articles.title: Why Mamdani opposes RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat's NYC event
articles.content: Zohran Mamdani called the Hindu nationalist group's ideology "exclusionary" ahead of Mohan Bhagwat's New York event. But can the mayor do anything to stop it? New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Tuesday he does not support an upcoming event featuring Mohan Bhagwat, chief of the Hindu nationalist group Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS), though he acknowledged the city likely has no power to stop it. Bhagwat is scheduled to speak Saturday at Madison Square Garden as part of what organizers are calling the "Universal Oneness Celebration," an event expected to draw around 5,000 attendees, local media reported. It is part of a broader global outreach tour tied to the RSS's centenary year, wherein Bhagwat is visiting the United States, Canada and the UK. When asked whether the event should be canceled at a press conference, Mamdani said: "I don't support the rally, but I don't know if the city has any jurisdiction on canceling a private event." Mamdani is the first Muslim and Indian American mayor in New York City's history. He added that his opposition to the visit reflected his role leading a city that believes in "the belonging of each and every person, no matter their color, their creed, their religion, their faith, wherever they're from." His mother is acclaimed Indian filmmaker Mira Nair. He added that he grew up with an understanding of India as "a pluralistic society of a secular Republic that believed in the belonging of each and every person who was from India." "It has been incredibly troubling to see the rise of a movement that is predicated on an exclusionary vision." The event is organized by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue, which says it has backing from over 135 Hindu American organizations and is meant to promote shared heritage and interfaith unity. However, several interfaith and civil rights groups – including Hindus for Human Rights, the Indian American Muslim Council and the Interfaith Center of New York – have criticized the event over Bhagwat's involvement and the RSS's history. They held a news conference outside New York City Hall calling for the event to be canceled. "Mohan Bhagwat does not represent Hindus. He leads an extremist Hindu nationalist movement that has fueled violence, exclusion and fear for minority communities," said Sravya Tadepalli, Deputy Executive Director of Hindus for Human Rights, in a statement. "New York should not provide the RSS with a stage on which religious nationalism can be repackaged as unity." The Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh, or RSS, is a right-wing Hindu organization founded by Keshav Baliram Hedgewar in 1925. Also referred to as the Sangh, it is Hindi for National Volunteer Organization. The group describes itself as a "Hindu-centric civilizational, cultural movement" focused on uniting Hindus and disputes accusations that it promotes intolerance. The RSS is the ideological parent of Prime Minister Narendra Modi's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), and the prime minister has had a longstanding association with the organization. In recent years, the organization has launched a global campaign to counter perceptions that it is a paramilitary group involved in violence against minority communities. To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video However, days earlier, the US Commission on International Religious Freedom urged sanctions against the RSS and asked the American government not to extend diplomatic courtesies to RSS members. The US government advisory body called the RSS an "umbrella organization whose sub-groups have perpetrated attacks on religious minorities, including Christians and Muslims." United Nations bodies and human rights groups have also pointed to a rise in abuses against India's religious minorities in recent years, citing hate speech, a religion-based citizenship law, demolitions of Muslim-owned properties, the revocation of autonomy for Muslim-majority Kashmir, and more. India's BJP-led government denies any discriminatory intent, pointing to programs such as food subsidies and electrification initiatives, which it says benefit all communities. The organization has been banned in India on multiple occasions, including in 1948 after a Hindu nationalist who had ties with the RSS assassinated independence leader Mahatma Gandhi. articles.title: Mamdani ‘heartbroken’ after Brooklyn building collapse
articles.content: Find our headlines more quickly in Google search results. Eight people have died and at least 17 were injured after a three-story building in Flatbush, Brooklyn, collapsed into an adjacent construction site Wednesday afternoon, Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Thursday as rescue operations continued. “There are no words for a loss of this magnitude,” Mamdani said in a statement. “My heart is with the families and loved ones of those we have lost, those who are injured and everyone grieving today.” City officials urged people to avoid the area where the building collapsed, at Flatbush and Bedford avenues. They said New Yorkers unable to reach someone they believe may have been affected by the catastrophe should call 311, while those outside of the city should call 212-639-9675. Authorities were working to determine the cause of the collapse of the building at 1321 Flatbush Ave. into the open-pit construction site at 2625 Bedford Ave. around 4 p.m. Wednesday. A third building, at 1323 Flatbush Ave., was damaged in the incident, with footage from the scene showing the side of that building ripped off and rubble from the collapsed building below. “We have immediately launched a full investigation into how exactly this happened with our law enforcement partners, and we will be looking into all aspects of the building and the neighboring construction site,” Department of Buildings Commissioner Ahmed Tigani said in a video statement late Wednesday. Sign up for free morning headlines in your inbox. No paywall here. THE CITY is a free-to-read, independent newsroom covering the stories that help you understand NYC. Sign up to get our headlines in your inbox. The city has not yet released the names of the victims. DOB inspectors are on scene at a major building collapse near Flatbush Avenue in Brooklyn assisting with recovery operations and conducting structural stability inspections of nearby buildings. pic.twitter.com/UsdgQ9ABmj At a church across from the disaster site Thursday morning, an anguished woman sobbed as she learned her husband, a construction worker, had died in the collapse. While exiting the church, she fell onto the sidewalk and others helped her get up. Jose Gutierrez, a construction worker who came to the church to support the woman and the family, said he knew her husband from working at the same company. Gutierrez said the man’s body was extracted from the construction site around 6 a.m. “We stayed here all night,” he said. “I came here to see my friend. I wish the situation was good.” Officials said they were conducting structural stability inspections of nearby buildings. Multiple people were trapped when first responders arrived Wednesday at the scene, which drew more than 250 fire and emergency medical personnel. Emergency management officials and the Red Cross have opened a reception center for displaced residents at the Flatbush YMCA at 1401 Flatbush Ave., authorities said. Authorities said they shut down water mains around the site to facilitate the search and rescue operations, with about 100 buildings affected. articles.title: Sponsored Commentary: Building connection in divided times
articles.description: In 2015, after 15 years in combat zones as a Marine and in East Africa working to alleviate extreme poverty, Jake Harriman came home to the United States and barely recognized it. The veteran and nonprofit leader was alarmed to see that Americans were increasingly siloed, with few chances to meet people beyond their own […]
articles.content: Jake Harriman, who served in the U.S. Marine Corps, helped create The Brickyard, a veteran-led movement that works to strengthen communities and heal divisions through social connection, community service and civic education. (Photo by Toto Cullen)In 2015, after 15 years in combat zones as a Marine and in East Africa working to alleviate extreme poverty, Jake Harriman came home to the United States and barely recognized it. The veteran and nonprofit leader was alarmed to see that Americans were increasingly siloed, with few chances to meet people beyond their own circles and beliefs. Trust and communication were eroding between neighbors; partisan affiliations had become so central to how people saw themselves, it was shaping society in harmful ways. Differences were not leading to productive conversations; rather, they were pulling communities apart. “There was just this awful, bitter fear and hatred ripping the country apart,” said Harriman, who felt he needed to do something. He had served 7 1/2 years in the U.S. Marine Corps and was the founder and former CEO of Nuru International, a global nonprofit collective that strengthens rural livelihoods and market systems in low-income, fragile communities. Through Nuru International, he and his team had helped more than 500,000 people move out of extreme poverty and had raised more than $100 million to scale the organization. Having seen what a determined team with resourceful strategies could do abroad, Harriman wanted to know what one could do at home. He spent four months studying democracy reform initiatives and meeting civic leaders working on division and isolation. The result was The Brickyard, a veteran-led movement and nonprofit organization that works to strengthen communities and heal divisions through social connection, community service and civic education and engagement. Built by trusted members of local communities, The Brickyard was formed to strategically engage veterans in civic life and bring people together through shared democratic values. The Brickyard’s goal is to convene people from across the ideological spectrum to work side by side on service projects, fitness challenges and potluck dinners. Through these events, community members from diverse backgrounds and lived experiences sit side by side to make new connections and build stronger communities. Its strategy has already proven impactful: In 2023, Brickyard leaders in Glen Rose, Texas, organized a “Share the Love” community roast where locals gave away clothes, toys and other goods. More than 200 people attended. For Harriman, moments like this are how communities find a sense of shared purpose and rebuild — and this can ripple outward nationally. “Our long-term vision is that we want a Brickyard in every small town and city across the country. We want The Brickyard to be the new meeting place for America, the next generation of civic organization where Americans can come together in a safe environment and have dialogue and meaningful connection with people who are not like them,” he said. The Brickyard has grown quickly, from around 1,000 members in 2024 to nearly 40,000 across all 50 states in 2026. Harriman’s strategy for it took shape long before this, during his childhood in Whetsell Settlement, West Virginia, among 40 families who lived off the land, hunted for food and often worked several jobs to get by. These formative years in a low-income community in Appalachia gave him a chance to see what agency and social cohesion looked like. Years later, that childhood and his military service shaped how he understood extreme poverty: not as living on less than $1.25 a day, the World Bank’s threshold at the time, but as lacking the freedom to make lasting, meaningful choices for one’s own life. Those ideas also run through Harriman’s new book, “Rescuing the Idea of America,” which lays out five steps for individuals to help strengthen their communities: believe, serve, connect, lead and restore. Believe: It starts with hope. This means acknowledging how hard things are, said Harriman, while believing a better future can be built. Serve: From there, people must look outward, serving others instead of just themselves. “By doing that, we can develop a whole new level of trust,” he said. Connect: The hardest step, Harriman said, is to connect with people who don’t share our backgrounds or beliefs. This can mean meeting over coffee or collaborating on a shared project. “It’s really hard to hate somebody while they are swinging a hammer next to them and building something together for somebody in the community,” he said. Lead: Rather than waiting for the next candidate to fix the country’s problems, Harriman maintains that the solution should start with the person in the mirror. “All of us have to step forward to lead in this moment in servant leadership,” he said. Restore: Last is to restore agency to people who have lost their voice by providing access to education, healthcare, safe spaces and economic self-sufficiency. “It does not mean giving a handout. It means giving a hand up,” Harriman said. Built one on top of the other, Harriman believes these steps can unite Americans around shared values and bring the country closer to what he calls the idea of America: not a place or an object, but a promise that everyone has the freedom to make lasting, meaningful choices. Harriman says a community that has succeeded in The Brickyard’s vision is one where all its members are engaged in shaping their shared future.

Whitmer urges end to food tariffs as Michigan prices rise
articles.description: Since April 2025, the United States has raised import taxes on food supplies, fertilizer, and agricultural machinery. Michigan estimates those policies increased food prices by 3% that year.
articles.content: Ann selects a watermelon from the Capuchin Soup Kitchen food pantry amidst uncertainty around SNAP benefits due the federal government shutdown. We're identifying only by her first name, Ann, to protect her family's privacy.(Beenish Ahmed / Michigan Public)Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer is calling for an end to recent tariffs on the food supply chain.Since April 2025, the United States has raised import taxes on food supplies, fertilizer, and agricultural machinery. The Michigan Department of Agriculture and Rural Development estimates those policies increased food prices by 3% that year.Whitmer sent a letter to the U.S. Secretary of the Treasury this week blaming the federal policies for also reducing the state’s agricultural exports.“We need a federal trade policy that works with our allies, brings supply chains home, and makes life more affordable. Families deserve relief from rising prices on the essentials they depend on every day,” Whitmer said in a press release.Whitmer cited National Taxpayers Union Foundation data that suggest Michigan is paying some of the highest per-household costs because of federal tariffs.Michigan State University Professor David Ortega is a food economist. He said that’s, in part, because Michigan has some of the most agricultural diversity in the country.“We have hundreds of crops and livestock sectors here in the state of Michigan and we are very much interconnected with some of our major trading partners, especially just across the border in Canada,” Ortega said.The Treasury Department did not respond to a request for comment Wednesday afternoon. President Donald Trump has made tariffs a centerpiece of his agenda. He’s defended them as supporting American businesses.The Urban-Brookings Tax Policy Center estimates food-related tariffs have mostly ranged between five and close to 14 percent since Trump launched the policies last April.Ortega said it’s not an issue that will go away “overnight” without stability.“This is why it’s so important to ensure that the message is getting across that our approach to policy, the approach to uncertainty that’s been created within trade policy and other aspects have made it much more difficult for our producers, our businesses,” Ortega said.In her letter, Whitmer asked for the federal government to refund Michiganders for the extra money they’ve paid resulting from the tariffs.Ortega, however, said it could be tough to refund consumers that difference though since they don’t pay the tariffs themselves.“It’s hard to know what the actual burden is of that individual tariff on individual consumers. The tariffs are paid for by importers and exporting companies, and so that’s going to be much harder to really nail down,” Ortega said.On a federal level, suppliers have already struggled with this after the U.S. Supreme Court declared many of Trump’s initial tariffs illegal and ordered the government to pay back money it collected.

articles.title: Supporting research on AI and children’s safety
articles.description: OpenAI commits $2 million to research on AI and children’s safety. The work supports shared tools to measure risks and opportunities for young people.
articles.content: OpenAI pledges $2 million as part of a global effort to better understand AI’s impact on children and support their safety and wellbeing. Earlier this week at the Paris Peace Forum, OpenAI signed the Charter of Engagement for Safer AI for Children(opens in a new window) and committed $2 million to support the scientific research network under the Coalition for Children’s Rights and Protection in the Age of AI. This builds on our call for global standards on youth AI safety, and sustained collaboration among governments, researchers, civil society and industry to translate shared evidence into practical safeguards. Our contribution supports shared measurement work: developing tools researchers can use to better understand and measure AI’s risks and opportunities for children, helping inform safer products and better policy. The charter sets out shared principles for safe, age-appropriate AI, alongside a research programme and safeguards for its independence. Research teams retain control over their conclusions, and findings will be published, including negative or inconclusive results. This work will help build the evidence needed to support the benefits of AI for young people while addressing risks to their safety and development. It builds on our support for comprehensive youth AI safety legislation that establishes strong, enforceable protections while preserving access to tools for learning, creativity and opportunity. Such frameworks should include age-appropriate safeguards by default, tools for parents, regular risk assessments and mitigation, and meaningful accountability. We look forward to engaging with European policymakers as the EU Kids Act develops, and with partners around the world to advance stronger protections and opportunities for young people.

articles.title: Gilbert + Tobin rethinks the business of law with AI
articles.description: A conversation with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin.
articles.content: A conversation with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin. Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI. Gilbert + Tobin(opens in a new window) is one of Australia’s leading corporate law firms, with work spanning capital markets, mergers and acquisitions, disputes, and technology. The firm operates in a profession built on specialist knowledge, careful judgement, and the secure handling of sensitive information. Gilbert + Tobin began by giving its people room to experiment with AI, then introduced ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT Work and Codex to move from individual assistance to defined, multistep agentic workflows, with people responsible for review and approval. We spoke with Sam Nickless, Partner and Chief Executive Officer at Gilbert + Tobin, about leading adoption from the front, where he’s seeing the value of AI, and his advice for other CEOs. We have three objectives: to use AI to deliver better services to our clients, make Gilbert + Tobin a great place to work for our people and firmly establish ourselves as a leader in our market. The real value we’ve seen from AI so far hasn’t been about reducing cost or needing fewer people, but freeing our people to focus on the more human side of their work, meeting with clients, coaching their teams and mentoring the future leaders of our industry. “It’s been about…freeing them up to then do the more human side of their work.” When ChatGPT first became available, we encouraged people to experiment with it and think about where it might create value. We were clear that no client data or confidential information should be entered. That gave people a safe, constrained environment to experiment. The next step was to provide a secure channel to powerful AI. We introduced ChatGPT Enterprise in a controlled environment and expanded from there. Australian data residency, contractual protections, role-based access and administrative controls gave us the confidence to scale while meeting our requirements and those of our clients. Governance should enable responsible use. Our message was simple: AI is not cheating. It is another tool people can use to apply their judgement. They still need to define the task, check the output and take responsibility for the final work. Leaders have to use the technology themselves: experiment, push the boundaries and learn what works. When people see that AI matters to you, it sets the tone and encourages others to engage with it. We did not mandate usage targets. Instead, we made the technology relevant. Our business transformation team demonstrated workflows tailored to different functions, while videos, showcases, challenges and an early AI bounty surfaced ideas from across the firm. Gilbert + Tobin has always been willing to lean into new technology. What has been most encouraging is the creativity coming from every part of the organisation – not only the technology team. “Getting started yourself…sets the tone and encourages others.” To help manage my workload more effectively, I created a “digital twin” through a custom GPT (now shifting to Plugins) using examples of my writing, feedback I had received, context about the firm and the way I like to work. It started as a tool for me and became more valuable when I shared it with my direct reports. My team is now able to use it to get “my feedback”, effectively, via ChatGPT. It lets them test their thinking against my context and working style before coming to me. It does not make decisions or speak for me; it helps our conversations start from a stronger place. I also used ChatGPT Work in a confidential annual review process involving our 120 partners. I asked it to update files with data from a spreadsheet, create PDFs and bundle the finished material. It completed the work in minutes. With a product as powerful as ChatGPT Work, it’s important to have the right admin controls behind the scenes, and it now provides detailed, granular data on usage. When I checked the usage dashboard afterwards, the cost for that annual review work was about $62. That was a good trade for the time I saved – and for work that would otherwise have required several other people over multiple days. Start by using the technology yourself. Experiment with real work, understand its limitations and show your people that learning matters. Pair that leadership with clear governance and practical enablement. Give teams examples tailored to their roles, create safe ways to test ideas and keep people responsible for the result. The opportunity is bigger than doing the same work a little more quickly. Used well, AI can raise the quality and volume of what an organisation produces – and give people more time for the complex, strategic work where their expertise and judgement create the greatest value. MOCAD celebrates 20 years of contemporary art in Detroit
articles.description: For 20 years, the Museum of Contemporary Art Detroit — or MOCAD — has been a home for experimental art, new ideas, and some of the city's most interesting artists.
articles.content: MOCAD artists from past and present exhibits gathered for a homecoming brunch to celebrate the museum's 20th anniversary. (VisualsByCaro)For 20 years, the Museum of Contemporary Art Detroit — or MOCAD — has been a home for experimental art, new ideas, and some of the city's most interesting artists. And it's become an important place where local creatives come into conversation with artists from around the world. You'd be just as likely to see something from a Detroit artist like Backpack Durden as artist Kara Walker.The museum is marking its 20th anniversary with a major exhibition called A Practice of Multiplicity, which has a community opening event this Saturday. The exhibit features work from more than 80 artists and looks back at the people, ideas and communities that have shaped MOCAD for two decades.Stateside spoke with the co-director and artistic director of MOCAD Jova Lynne about the exhibit and the unique place MOCAD holds in the Detroit art world. An edited excerpt of that conversation is below and you can click on the audio player above to hear the whole conversation.This conversation has been edited for clarity and length. April Baer: What comes up for you about the evolution of the museum over that time? You have not been at the museum that entire time. But but maybe some thoughts on what's special about it and what's central to its identity? Jova Lynne: I would say, in institutional life, we’re a toddler, because usually institutions have very, very long, long lives. And I think being a toddler is really amazing because we get to rebel and be a little different, which is inherently a part of the story of MOCAD. So in 1996, an art critic and art writer for the Detroit Free Press named Marsha Miro had this idea where she was like, why don't we have a contemporary art museum in Detroit? At that time, we had already sort of been living through the legacy of the Cass Corridor Arts movement, which is a movement that's definitely born and bred of Detroit, that sort of is underrepresented in the larger arts field. And we had this great legacy of, alongside that movement, a great movement that doesn't actually really have a name, but I would say a great movement of Detroit artists, specifically a group of Black artists who really rallied together to make sure that Black artists could have not only representation in terms of galleries, but also in terms of artists supporting other artists in their career. So you had all of these artists who were making, making, making and no place to showcase their work.In Detroit, MOCAD, to this day is the only contemporary art museum. And when I say contemporary art, I mean focusing on artists who are alive or have recently been alive, making work that speaks to the different cultural moments of our time. That includes social political moments. That includes big questions of our futures, as well as sort of reconciling with our past. And so Marsha had this idea, and it took her about 10 years to build the museum. She was working in very close partnership with her other two cofounders, Julia Reyes Taubman, who was a great photographer and philanthropist people mover, as well as Susanne Feld Hilberry, who had one of the more established galleries in the area.AB: At the same time, one of the things I've been thinking about with 20 years of MOCAD is just how much the city has been going through. Are there particular exhibitions or artists that you feel have contributed to the modern definition of of what MOCAD has to show and reflect back to the city?JL: Certainly. I mean, I think this show specifically was a really hard one to curate. MOCAD has showcased hundreds and thousands of artists. And so it was really hard, to be honest, to narrow down this artist list and really think about.I broke the show up into four different parts to speak to the different ways that artists engage with Detroit, but also the legacy of the museum building itself up. And it's kind of a call and response with the history of the city, I would say the history of the state, the history of our world. And so it's interesting to have this museum emerge during a time of such incredible economic uncertainty. And I go back to that sort of rebellious spirit that we know lives within Detroit, the rebellious spirit of artists, and also the possibilities for the future that existed then. And I think something that's really special about MOCAD — because we're kind of an unruly melting pot of different people, places and things — we're able to show works that maybe are a little bit more unconventional.I think usually when an artist creates, they're known for one specific thing. But one thing I like about MOCAD is when we work with more established artists, we end up showing things that maybe the commercial landscape is less interested in, and that's something I'm really proud of.I also feel like we have this kind of exchange across generations. So we did a major retrospective of Olayami Dabls’ work. You know, he has a rich legacy of mentorship here in the city. And we have a piece by the artist Bryce Detroit, who certainly has been mentored by him. The late Gilda Snowden, who mentored LaKela Brown, who's also in the show. You know, it's just such a beautiful thing. And Lenny Sinclair, we did a major retrospective of her work called Motor City Underground. We’re reprinting the catalogue for that exhibition. I'm super proud of it. She is in the show too, and it's just this beautiful exchange.AB: So when we're having this conversation again in 20 years, what would you hope people would say about MOCAD and its impact on Detroit and the broader arts scene globally? JL: You know, I will say that 20 years from now, I hope that anybody can come into the museum, and not just see themselves in it, but see the potential of community. I think that something that I'm really proud of is our education and community engagement programming, where artists are still at the forefront of the institution and guiding those sort of ideas for how we interpret work.I think in 20 years, I want to have grown the museum so that you can recognize this from anywhere around the town, anywhere around the state. And I want to continue to be a place that fosters radical ideas because people thought Marsha [Miro] was crazy when she was, like, going around saying, we need contemporary. Everybody said, well, we have the DIA. Why do we need something else? And it's not that we need something else, it's that we need something different. And it's the diversity of ideas and of artwork that makes this city so great.There's two neon works at MOCAD. There's one by Martin Creed that says “Everything is going to be all right.” That's on the front. And then on the back of the museum, there's a new piece that says “Artists must be able to create at the same scale that society has to destroy.” And I think that for me, MOCAD is that place of duality where everything is going to be all right. And as long as we give artists the tools and access that we need to create, to display, to engage with community, to exhibit, to have hard conversations, then everything really will be all right.

articles.title: College rates down in Michigan, even with cheap tuition. Can billboards help?
articles.description: The battle to increase college graduation rates is going for hearts and minds with a $5 million ad campaign that hopes to combat anti-college narratives.
articles.content: Leaders are working to convince Michiganders of the value of a postsecondary education The state has invested millions in tuition assistance for young people and adults, but enrollment has not changed significantly since then A massive messaging campaign has begun as part of the first step in changing attitudes, which many say is necessary for the state to prosper Along M-36 in Whitmore Lake, commuters now can see a new billboard: “In Italy, there’s a museum of spaghetti and in Michigan, two years of college is free.” The billboard is one of many that have popped up across the state, along with ads on television and social media, as part of a $5 million campaign that aims to change attitudes about the value of college. The campaign, funded by foundations and taxpayers, intends to raise awareness of three state-funded college scholarships for adults and traditional students to earn a certificate, associate degree or bachelor degree. It’s the first step of work to change Michigan’s college-going culture and similar to one decades ago to normalize the idea that everyone needs a high school diploma, said Doug Ross, co-manager of Level Up Michigan! The bipartisan group of business, labor and education leaders is working to increase the education and skill level of residents. “It took us most of the 20th century to establish the conventional wisdom that people ought to get a high school degree,” said Ross. “The new conventional wisdom we need: Young people today require education and skill beyond high school to build a family-supporting career.” A record-low 31% of Americans consider a college education “very important,” down from 70% in 2013, according to an October poll by Gallup. RELATED: Michigan college enrollment rate slips, despite $1B in state scholarships Michigan voters are skeptical of EVs and the value of college in new poll Michigan spent $49M to send essential workers to college. Few chose to attend Confidence in higher education has cratered, said Zach Hrynowski, senior education researcher at Gallup. Other polls show Americans still value higher education and the financial security it brings, along with other benefits such as mental and physical well-being and the likelihood of being employed in a job where the individual finds purpose, Hrynowski said. “You can have confidence and trust and value in a product and not be confident in the seller of it very much,” said Hrynowski. Polls show confidence in higher education has dropped because of cost, campus climate limiting the expression of speech and questions about whether what’s being taught is relevant to the workplace, Hrynowski said.Donate The average published price of Michigan’s 15 public universities cost $17,105, in 2025-26, nearly double the inflation-adjusted average in 2001-02, though most students pay far less because of financial aid. The return on college investment “far exceeds the costs,” even with earnings adjusted for student loan debt, according to research by the Brookings Institution, a nonprofit public policy organization. Those armed with a degree on average earn $8,000 more annually than individuals without a credential, even after accounting for student debt. Michigan has invested more than $1 billion in three major scholarships since 2023 to help traditional students and adults earn a certificate, associate degree or bachelor degree as part of its goal to arm 60% of residents with a postsecondary credential by 2030. Despite the investment, the percentage of adults with postsecondary degrees or certificates has only increased to 51.6% of adults from 49.1% in 2019 when Gov. Gretchen Whitmer took office. During that time, enrollment at Michigan’s public universities and community colleges has declined 12% to 555,000 in 2025, according to the Michigan Association of State Universities. Part of the problem, college boosters think, is that polling shows 70% of residents are unaware of the scholarships. “Michigan’s policy work is done, in large part,” said Sandy Baruah, CEO and president of Detroit Regional Chamber, which is a partnerof Level Up Michigan!. “We’ve made (community college) tuition free for everybody. Yet we are not seeing cultural success. Now, we need to have cultural attitudes change.” Did you know? Getting people’s attention about fried chicken in Georgia is part of a campaign to tell them about two years of free college in Michigan. (Courtesy of Perich Advertising + Design ) An August poll by the Glengariff Group asked Michigan adults whether education beyond high school is required to prepare a young person for a career. Nearly 50% either said no, they’re not sure or it depends. That is a problem because there is “an anti-college myth in the ethos right now,” said Ryan Fewins-Bliss, president of the Michigan College Access Network, another Level Up Michigan! partner. Attempts to counter that messaging to individuals have included messaging around the fact that college degrees lead to increased earning potential, but that doesn’t seem to be resonating, he added. “We are trying to find the right messaging to help people get out of this anti-college funk,” said Fewins-Bliss. The public’s attitude also does not line up with industry needs, where research by TalentFirst, a coalition of business leaders in west Michigan, shows that 70% of jobs require a postsecondary credential. “The level of knowledge and skill that employers are needing is continually being raised as technology, automation and business processes increased the need for a more educated and skilled workforce,” said Kevin Stotts, president of TalentFirst, another Level Up Michigan! partner. “So we have to have the culture.” Level Up Michigan!’s awareness campaign began in September and will last through January 2028. The ads hope to increase awareness of the scholarships from 3 in 10 Michigan residents to 8 in 10, said Craig Dunaway, director of client services for Perich Advertising + Design in Ann Arbor, which is handling the campaign. The ads also include a link to a webpage, 2yearsfree.com, which exposes viewers to the two-year scholarships, connects them to a local community college and more. A second phase of the campaign planned to launch next year will target graduating high school students with information and testimonials to increase the postsecondary enrollment rate. The goal is 70% for the class of 2029, which would be an increase from about 50%. “They can’t take advantage of it if they don’t know it exists,” Dunaway said. “These are programs that can change people’s lives. We want them to be aware of them.” Level Up Michigan! is working to raise the largest amount of funding, $4.2 million, with support so far from several foundations including the Kresge Foundation, Skillman Foundation, Frey Foundation, Mott Foundation,Steelcase Foundation, Kellogg Foundation, Michigan Community College Association and more. It also has benefitted from$250,000 in state funds awarded to the Diploma Equity Project, the fiscal agent for Level Up Michigan!, from the Michigan Department of Lifelong Education, Advancement, and Potential to expand the state’s outreach on higher education opportunities and its value. The state agency also awarded $250,000 each to the Michigan College Access Network and Michigan Adult, Community and Alternative Education Association to raise awareness. “These partnerships will help more learners pursue their goals, strengthen families and build the skilled workforce Michigan needs to thrive,” said Beverly Walker-Griffea, executive director of the state Department of Lifelong Education, Advancement, and Potential. The campaigns come as Michigan’s per capita income has plummeted nationally from 19th in 2000 to 39th in 2025, median family income has fallen from 106% of the national average in 2000 to 91% today and the state ranks 39th in the nation for the percentage of residents with a postsecondary credential. Michigan residents need to see that getting an education beyond high school is normal and necessary and the state helps with costs, Ross said. “If we don’t change that,” Ross said, “Michigan will continue to fall behind the nation economically on all the important economic measures.”

Turkey’s president calls the war in Gaza an ‘ecocide’ at the UN climate summit
articles.description: Turkey’s president calls the war in Gaza an ‘ecocide’ at the UN climate summit AP News Erdogan calls Gaza war an ‘ecocide’ at UN climate summit; Israel: ‘Campaign of lies’ The Times of Israel Türkiye slams Israel's baseless accusations against Erdoğan | Daily Sabah Daily Sabah Turkey spotlights Gaza ‘ecocide’ at UN climate talks dominated by fossil fuel producers Financial Times Israel excluded from COP31 climate sum
articles.content: Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan on Wednesday called for the world to recognize the environmental impacts of the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza and asked the Israeli government to grant more aid access to the Palestinian territory. Erdogan was speaking at the U.N. climate summit, known as COP31, in Antalya, Turkey. “What has taken place in Gaza is not only a genocide, but it is also an ecocide,” Erdogan said to applause by world leaders and other climate envoys. A U.N.-backed panel of independent experts concluded last year that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Israel vehemently denies the allegations and has accused the panel of antisemitism. “Centuries old olive trees have been cut down. The soil and water have been polluted in Gaza, and cities in Gaza have been turned into enormous piles of rubble,” Erdogan said. “With Gaza’s destroyed infrastructure, compounded by torrential rain and by flooding, tens of thousands of tents and shelters have been inundated.” Turkey President Recep Tayyip Erdogan speaks at the COP31 U.N. Climate Summit, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. (AP Photo/Khalil Hamra) Turkey President Recep Tayyip Erdogan speaks at the COP31 U.N. Climate Summit, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, in Antalya, Turkey. (AP Photo/Khalil Hamra) Israel’s Foreign Ministry responded in a post on X, accusing Erdogan of “using an international forum to push his anti-Israel campaign of lies” and of supporting Hamas. Israel launched its campaign in Gaza following attacks by Hamas-led militants in southern Israel on Oct. 7, 2023. Militants killed around 1,200 people and took 251 hostages. “Those who truly care about Gaza should demand that Hamas disarm so reconstruction can begin,” the statement read. Israel wasn’t invited to COP31. Israel’s retaliatory offensive has killed more than 74,000 people, according to local health authorities, and destroyed much of Gaza. The Health Ministry, part of Gaza’s Hamas-run government, doesn’t distinguish between civilians and combatants, but says women and children make up nearly half of the dead. Erdogan has been an outspoken critic of Israel, while Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has called Erdogan an antisemitic “tyrant.” “The latest country to become a superspreader of antisemitic lies is Turkey,” Netanyahu said in September while speaking at the U.N. General Assembly. Displaced Palestinians walk through a rain-soaked tent camp following heavy rainfall in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza Strip, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026. (AP Photo/Abdel Kareem Hana) Displaced Palestinians walk through a rain-soaked tent camp following heavy rainfall in Deir al-Balah, central Gaza Strip, Saturday, Nov. 7, 2026. (AP Photo/Abdel Kareem Hana) In recent days, heavy rainfall and subsequent flooding destroyed many of the tents and makeshift shelters that Palestinian residents now live in. At least four people were killed earlier this week when a sand embankment collapsed on their shelter. The rain also left many displaced people without food, drinking water or a dry place to sleep. Humanitarian aid enters the territory, but imports remain far below levels before the start of the Israel-Hamas war — and many items remain blocked by Israel. A 2025 report by the U.N. Environment Program also outlined the devastating reality of Gaza’s environment since the war began. Remote sensing assessments showed that by May 2025, more than 97% of the tree crops, 82% of annual crops, 95% of shrubland and 89% of grass and fallow land had been damaged, according to the UNEP report. “As of now, our families only have 3% of cropland to use, and that is assuming it’s distributed across 2 million Palestinians” in the Gaza Strip, said Mohammed Usrof, co-founder and executive director of the Palestinian Institute for Climate Strategy. “Not talking about these losses undermines Palestinians’ food supply, livelihoods and ability to remain on their land,” Usrof said. Palestinians walk through a tent camp housing displaced people amid buildings destroyed by Israeli strikes during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza City, Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. (AP Photo/Jehad Alshrafi) Palestinians walk through a tent camp housing displaced people amid buildings destroyed by Israeli strikes during the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza City, Sunday, Nov. 8, 2026. (AP Photo/Jehad Alshrafi) The territory’s ability to dispose of garbage, treat sewage and deliver clean water has been virtually decimated by three years of war. This has made grim living conditions worse and raised health risks for hundreds of thousands of people deprived of adequate shelter, food and medicine, aid groups say. The conflict has “all but eliminated” Gazan fishing livelihoods, the report said, highlighting how marine ecosystems have been contaminated with munitions, sewage and solid waste. “For people in Gaza, this translates into severely limited access to safe drinking water, greater exposure to waterborne diseases and toxic substances, deepening food insecurity and the loss of livelihoods dependent on agriculture and fishing,” Ghiwa Nakat, executive director at Greenpeace MENA, told The Associated Press. Nakat also warned that Gaza’s environment could take years to recover. “The environmental damage will not end when the war ends,” Nakat said. “Contaminated soil and groundwater, destroyed ecosystems and the collapse of essential environmental infrastructure could undermine public health, food security and livelihoods for generations, threatening communities’ resilience and their ability to recover.” World leaders began formal talks at COP31 this week, seeking agreement on concrete steps to curb global warming after a year of deadly floods, heat waves and other climate-related disasters. More than 70 world leaders and senior government officials are speaking at the summit, though some key leaders are absent, including heads of state from the United States, China and India. articles.content: Nvidia’s board is preparing to dismiss CEO Jensen Huang following a report from The New York Times about a second alleged extramarital affair, just days after he admitted to a separate affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy, The Wall Street Journal reports. The second alleged affair was with an executive who reports to him, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, Kimberly Powell, according to the Times. The Nvidia board will meet as soon as Wednesday night to decide on Huang’s future at the company, according to the Journal. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Verge. On Thursday morning, Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation, saying CFO Colette Kress has been appointed interim CEO. Huang and Powell, who are both married to other people, were allegedly captured together at a hotel in San Jose during Nvidia’s GTC developer conference in March, two unnamed sources told the Times. The Times has not seen the video. Rumors about a potential affair between the two had long circulated at Nvidia, an unnamed source told CNBC, partially because Powell does not have a health or science background. Nvidia’s stock fell more than 7 percent in after-hours trading Wednesday. Since Nvidia and Huang confirmed an extramarital relationship with Megaspeed executive and alleged spy Alice Huang and a subsequent investigation over the weekend, the company has said it retained former US attorney Joon H. Kim and his firm, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, to handle it, but today’s rumor suggests it won’t wait for those results to act. Last year, Huang hired crisis communications firm Heller known for handling public sex scandals, according to Wired. Its founder has advised several powerful men who faced public scrutiny, Wired reported, like former congressman Anthony Weiner and writer Jeffrey Toobin. Heller did not immediately respond to a request for comment from The Verge. Update, November 12th: Added note that Huang has now resigned.

articles.title: ‘The 120th Congress is coming’: Dems who flipped the US House pack freshman orientation
articles.description: WASHINGTON — With a sweeping majority secured in the U.S. House next Congress, newly elected Democrats arrived in the nation’s capital this week vowing to act on their agenda of affordability and accountability. The dozens of Democrats who flipped the House majority are in Washington, D.C., for several days as part of new member orientation. […]
articles.content: Democratic and Republican members-elect of the U.S. House, along with staff, participate in new member orientation at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., on Nov. 9, 2026. (Photo by Shauneen Miranda/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — With a sweeping majority secured in the U.S. House next Congress, newly elected Democrats arrived in the nation’s capital this week vowing to act on their agenda of affordability and accountability. The dozens of Democrats who flipped the House majority are in Washington, D.C., for several days as part of new member orientation. The onboarding tradition for both parties features training sessions and programming, as well as a class photo on the U.S. Capitol steps and a room lottery to determine their office spaces. In early January, the new members will be sworn in, and Democrats will spend the next two years attempting to deliver on the issues they spent months campaigning on — ranging from lowering the high cost of healthcare to enacting anti-corruption efforts to trying to overturn the GOP’s mega tax and spending cut law. Their introduction was overwhelming at times. Rep.-elect J.D. Ford, the Democrat who will represent Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, said orientation is “definitely like drinking from a fire hose, but I’m just trying to take it day by day.’’ Ford said he’s “really excited to make some relationships,” noting that “obviously this building is all about that, so this has been really good for us to not just meet members of my own party, but potential members I could work across the aisle with.” Rep.-elect Oliver G. Gilbert III, set to represent Florida’s historically Black-dominated 24th Congressional District, said “we have a lot to do, but I know we’re up to the task. “This country is 250 years old, and we’re the greatest country in the history of the world, but our greatness is always tomorrow, it’s not yesterday, so it’s what we make it, and so, we’re going to make it something better in this Congress,” he said. “The 120th Congress is coming.” The blue tsunami During the programming, States Newsroom got a glimpse into the top priorities of several incoming Democratic members, who are riding on the heels of a blue tsunami that swept the country on Election Day and also flipped the U.S. Senate. At least 75 new House Democrats, excluding non-voting delegates, have been elected as of Wednesday afternoon, The Associated Press projected, with 12 races to be called. Democrats will control at least 255 seats in the House, according to the AP. House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York — the likely speaker in the new Congress — would helm Democrats’ legislative agenda if elected by his peers. But with more than two years left in office, President Donald Trump is all but certain to veto many of Democrats’ measures, potentially making the party’s work more of a messaging exercise ahead of the 2028 presidential election. Still, Democratic members-elect who made a new majority laid out the visions they are eager to deliver on in the next Congress, fueled by voters’ concerns in their districts: Florida Gilbert, set to represent the Sunshine State’s 24th Congressional District, wants to “make the American dream more accessible,” pointing to affordability and accountability as the avenue to those aims. “When I talk to people, it doesn’t matter whether you’re speaking Haitian Creole, you’re speaking Spanish, you’re speaking English, they’re all worried about the price of gas, the accessibility of healthcare, the lack of affordable, quality housing, how your kids are going to be educated, whether the American dream is still going to be accessible to them,” Gilbert said. Indiana Ford, who unseated incumbent Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz, said he heard “over and over again” from voters in the district that they were “really tired of seeing the grift from this administration.” He also cited healthcare accessibility and broader affordability as other major priorities. “Cost of utilities, groceries, you name it — people are actually talking about it at their kitchen dinner table, so I think moving forward, still trying to get my sea legs here, but we need to address those issues in this next Congress when we get back here in January,” Ford said. Maryland For Rep.-elect Adrian Boafo of Maryland, addressing the Trump administration’s major downsizing of the federal workforce and its effects on constituents in his 5th Congressional District marks a priority for him heading into Congress. “Federal workers have been downright assaulted by this administration,” said Boafo, who is succeeding and previously served as an aide to retiring Democratic Rep. Steny Hoyer. “Frankly, we’ve got to find a pathway to not just rehire the people who, in my opinion, were illegally fired — we also have to provide some oversight as to what happened with DOGE,” Boafo added, pointing to an earlier initiative under the Trump administration that sought to drastically reduce federal government spending and resulted in mass firings across agencies, hitting Marylanders hard in particular. Michigan Rep.-elect Donavan McKinney, set to represent Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, said overturning the GOP’s mega tax and spending cut law, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” is top of mind for him heading into Congress. “What I’m hearing every single day from my residents, they’re getting letters in the mail as we speak … that they’re going to get kicked off food assistance, their healthcare,” said McKinney, whose district is among the poorest in the country and includes parts of Detroit. Nebraska Rep.-elect Denise Powell, who will represent Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District, said “we need to get a farm bill passed as soon as humanly possible,” pointing to the long overdue agriculture aid and nutrition programs package that has stalled amid partisan disputes. Powell, who will be the first Latina to represent Nebraska in Congress after flipping the seat of retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon, pointed to healthcare as another priority heading into Congress. For Powell, part of that includes wanting to reverse the Medicaid cuts baked into the tax and spending cut law, which axes roughly $1 trillion in program spending over 10 years. Wisconsin Rep.-elect Mitchell Berman said his No. 1 priority is to deliver on the needs of constituents in his southeastern Wisconsin district, which includes “lowering costs of living, making sure that folks can afford to put food on the table, pay their rent and also healthcare.” As a registered nurse, Berman said with that background he wants to “make sure we can make healthcare affordable for folks.” Berman flipped Wisconsin’s 1st Congressional District after defeating incumbent GOP Rep. Bryan Steil. The district has not seen a Democrat hold the seat in more than three decades. Also in the Badger State, Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke said she’s focused on fulfilling the campaign promises she ran on, including “lowering healthcare costs — making sure it’s affordable and accessible — combating corruption really on both sides of the aisle, delivering for our agricultural communities by ending the war in Iran, changing what we do with tariffs.” Cooke flipped Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District after beating incumbent GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in another upset for Republicans.

articles.content: (Steve Carmody / Michigan Public )Michigan gasoline prices have been dropping essentially since Election Day. The same is true of diesel prices, but not as much.AAA Michigan said as of Wednesday, the average price for a gallon of regular unleaded gasoline in Michigan was hovering around four dollars. The price of a gallon of gas has dropped 40 cents since the day after the election.Michigan diesel prices have also declined, but only by 19 cents during the same period. Analysts said the decline is likely tied to the switch to a cheaper winter blend of gasoline, along with the hope for diplomacy with Iran and increased crude oil shipments from the Persian Gulf.But industry analyst Patrick DeHaan points to seasonal factors behind most of the decline.“Americans simply don’t drive as much in colder weather,” DeHaan told ABC News, “Refineries are processing more oil, and there’s more gasoline and diesel as a result of that.”DeHaan adds the future of the price decline depends in part on whether President Donald Trump re-escalates tensions with Iran.

articles.title: Old Detroit school district pays off decade-long operating debt as board transfers millage
articles.description: After voters approved a millage in August that will allow the Detroit school district to collect the revenue it needs to operate, the board authorized a summer tax levy beginning next July.
articles.content: This story also appeared in Chalkbeat Detroit Detroit’s public school district has taken a major step forward after years of debt and emergency management. Superintendent Nikolai Vitti on Tuesday announced that the operating debt held by Detroit Public Schools for the last decade has been paid off. At the same time, the school board approved transferring a millage levy to the Detroit Public Schools Community District. DPS, the legacy entity left over after the state split the district into two separate entities to tackle debt, took out a State Emergency Loan in 2016 and repaid it about a year and a half ahead of schedule, thanks to the 18-mill tax on non-homestead properties. Now that voters approved the 18-mill operating millage transfer in August, the Detroit Board of Education has authorized a summer tax levy beginning next July for businesses and people who own rental properties. The tax can be levied next summer and every year through 2045 and collected by the new entity, DPSCD. However, DPS still has capital debt. As of July, the total is $1.5 billion. DPS made interest payments of $24.3 million in October, according to district documents, and the district is scheduled to make a $139.2 million interest and principal payment in May. The debt is expected to be fully repaid in 2040, according to documents from Detroit City Council’s Legislative Policy Division. For most taxpayers in Michigan, summer taxes become a lien on July 1 each year and are due by September 14, while winter taxes become a lien on December 1 and are due on February 14. “By collecting the funds in July, the district will receive collections in the summer to support school operations until state funding is received in October,” board president LaTrice McClendon said. The operating millage was last renewed in 2024. A court decision earlier this year said DPS must cease collecting that tax with that operating debt nearing repayment. Now, DPSCD will have the authority to continue collecting the full operating funding available under Michigan’s school funding formula. Vitti said the old district made its final principal payment of $4.5 million and final interest payment of $27,000 in September. According to district documents, DPS’ remaining millage fund balance of $190.8 million will be transferred to DPSCD. The school board held a special meeting Tuesday evening to discuss the tax levy and then approved the resolution during its regular board meeting later that night. As a new taxing entity, DPSCD had to adopt a resolution to allow it to begin collecting the millage funds. The $112 million the millage will collect in 2026 is a fraction of the district’s overall $1.1 billion budget. But the revenue is critical to the school system. Vitti previously said that the estimated revenue generated by the tax levy would constitute $2,400 of the $10,300 per pupil the district receives from the state. DPSCD was created in 2016 as part of a legislative initiative to address mounting debt in DPS. The new district had a debt-free start to handle day-to-day school administration, while DPS stayed intact to collect taxes to pay off operating and capital debts of $3.2 billion. Since DPSCD would not receive local property tax revenue, the state then filled the gap with money from the 1998 Tobacco Settlement Fund. “DPSCD, like every other district in Michigan, has its own local funding revenue and is no longer relying on tobacco settlement money for its local taxation starting the next fiscal year,” Vitti said Tuesday. Chalkbeat Detroit Bureau Chief Lori Higgins and reporter Hannah Dellinger contributed to this report.

articles.content: The accused killer of a Warren woman has chosen to not be present for his trial that started this week and was denied in his attempt to fire his attorney as the trial approached. The first-degree murder trial of Deandre Howard Booker, 34, of Roseville, began Tuesday with jury selection that is scheduled to continue Thursday in Macomb County Circuit Court for the death of his ex-girlfriend, Ashley Elkins, 30, a mother and hair stylist who went missing Jan. 2, 2025. Court was closed Wednesday for Veterans Day. Once a jury is selected, the prosecution will present an opening statement, and the defense can make an opening statement. Judge Teri Lynn Dennings on Tuesday granted Booker’s request to not be in the Mount Clemens courtroom or remotely view his trial proceedings, according to court records. Dennings also denied Booker’s multiple requests to fire his court-appointed attorney, Robbie Lang, an assistant county public defender, in the days leading up to the trial. Booker also was uncooperative at times during his multi-day preliminary examination in 2025 in 39th District Court. He refused to appear in court at least twice, yelled obscenities or made threats from his holding cell, including Booker saying, “F—ing let me go,” and refused to wear attire for court. He was accused by Assistant Macomb Prosecutor Carmen DeFranco of staring at and attempting to intimidate witnesses. Police and prosecutors believe Booker killed Elkins on Jan. 2 after luring her to his unit at Hampton Court Apartments on Pinehurst Street behind the Eastgate Shopping Center at Gratiot Avenue and Frazho Road, and transported her remains in a shopping cart to a neighboring apartment complex’s trash bin. Her remains have never been found despite a widespread search including Pine Tree Acres landfill in Lenox Township. First-degree murder carries a mandatory penalty of life without parole. A large volume of evidence against Booker was presented at his 2025 preliminary examination in 39th District Court in Roseville. Police say they found Elkins’ blood in several locations in Booker’s, including in the bathtub drain where they also found a bullet fragment, a clump of hair and Elkins’ earring. Her blood was found on a jacket collar that he wore and at the bottom of the trash bin where he allegedly dumped the body. Prosecutors presented security-video clips of a figure pushing a full shopping cart in his apartment and appearing to discard a heavy object into the side door of a trash bin at about 5 a.m. Jan. 3. Police say Booker then fled to stay with a friend in Flint, where he was initially arrested Jan. 8 and held until Jan. 31, when he was charged with first-degree murder, tampering with evidence, mutilation and disinterment of a body, and concealing the death of an individual. Elkin’s abandoned vehicle had been found Jan. 7 in the area of 13 Mile Road and Little Mack Avenue in Roseville. Roseville police Detective Chris Moran testified at the prior hearing that around the time of Elkins’ disappearance, Booker made several incriminating Google searches on his iPhone: “telling God I want to kill someone, 9 millimeter silencers in Roseville, murder out of rage, shooting a gun through a pillow, can you track a location when phone is off and what happens to trash.” Booker had also conducted computer searches on topics such as fastest routes from Flint to Ohio, what to do while on the run, is blood traceable and how to beat a polygraph test. He also attempted to delete his Google search history. Police found a sales record of Booker’s alleged purchase of a 9mm pistol at the Flint residence where he was arrested, police said. Elkins’ mother, Monika Elkins, and other family members and relatives have attended the court hearings. Elkins was the mother of two boys.

Ghana and partners review progress in pandemic fund-supported preparedness efforts
articles.content: Ghana and its partners have reviewed progress in strengthening the country’s capacity to prevent, detect and respond to public health threats during a mission by Dr Maggie Chase of the Pandemic Fund Secretariat from 5 to 9 October 2026. The mission brought together the World Health Organization (WHO) Ghana, the Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations (FAO), the Ghana Health Service (GHS), the Veterinary Services Directorate, academic and research institutions, and civil society organisations to assess implementation progress, identify challenges and agree on priorities for advancing Ghana’s Pandemic Fund-supported project. The project supports efforts to strengthen disease surveillance, laboratory systems and the health workforce, which are essential to detecting emerging threats early and mounting effective public health responses. During the mission, Dr Chase held discussions with the WHO Ghana Representative, Dr Fiona Braka, WHO and FAO implementation teams, and the Director-General of the Ghana Health Service. She also visited the National Public Health Reference Laboratory and engaged technical working groups and partners involved in surveillance, laboratory services and workforce development. Welcoming her to the WHO Ghana Country Office, Dr Fiona Braka said, “This mission provides an important opportunity for us, together with our partners, to take stock of progress made, review project timelines and identify how we can work more effectively to achieve our shared goals. We look forward to constructive discussions that will help maintain momentum and ensure the successful implementation of the project”. The Director-General of the Ghana Health Service, Dr Samuel Kaba Akoriyea, underscored the importance of translating project investments into sustainable improvements in the health system. “The Pandemic Fund provides an important opportunity to strengthen Ghana’s capacity to identify public health threats and respond effectively. Our priority is to ensure that the capacities developed through this support are integrated into the health system and sustained to protect the health of the population”, he said. A key component of the mission was a visit to the West African Centre for Cell Biology of Infectious Pathogens (WACCBIP), where Dr Chase reviewed progress in implementing activities supported by the Pandemic Fund. The engagement highlighted the training of 10 laboratory personnel in bioinformatics, an important investment in strengthening Ghana’s capacity for genomic surveillance, pathogen detection and analysis, and preparedness for emerging infectious disease threats. The Head of Department at WACCBIP, Professor Peter Quashie, emphasised the importance of developing local expertise in this specialised field. “Building bioinformatics capacity is critical to Ghana’s health security. This training will equip our laboratory personnel with the skills to analyse genomic data, track emerging pathogens, and generate evidence to guide public health decisions. By investing in local expertise, Ghana will be better positioned to detect and respond rapidly to infectious disease threats and strengthen its preparedness for future pandemics”, he said. The mission also included a visit to the School of Public Health at the University of Ghana, where Dr Chase met with the Dean and faculty members to discuss the institution’s contributions to the project's workforce development pillar. The School plays an important role in building the capacity of frontline, intermediate and advanced-level public health professionals across the sub-region. It also works with the Veterinary Services Directorate to promote a One Health approach to workforce development, recognising the links between human, animal and environmental health. Key achievements highlighted during the engagement included Geographic Information Systems (GIS) training, the development of training materials on humanitarian crises, validation of training modules and the delivery of several capacity-building programmes. The discussions also identified implementation challenges requiring attention. These included limited emphasis on cross-border activities, fragmentation and duplication across the project's three pillars, and insufficient clarity in roles and responsibilities within implementation arrangements, affecting coordination and efficiency. The findings pointed to the need for stronger integration across project components, clearer governance structures and improved coordination among implementing partners to maximise the impact of the investments. Beyond the institutional visits, the mission provided an opportunity to engage the Pandemic Fund Technical Coordination Group, technical working groups on surveillance, laboratories and health workforce, as well as civil society organisations and academic partners. Discussions focused on reviewing implementation progress, addressing operational bottlenecks and strengthening coordination among the institutions responsible for delivering project activities. The importance of collaboration across human and animal health was also emphasised, particularly in strengthening coordinated disease surveillance and emergency preparedness. Reflecting on the engagements, Maggie Chase of the Pandemic Fund said, “I am pleased with the progress I have seen and the opportunity to engage first-hand with the implementing agencies and partners driving this work. These engagements are important for understanding the progress made, addressing challenges and ensuring that the project achieves its intended goals”. The mission concluded with a debriefing to the Chief Director of the Ministry of Health, during which the findings were presented and priorities for continued implementation discussed. Through the Pandemic Fund-supported project, Ghana and its partners are working to strengthen the systems, technical expertise and institutional capacities needed to prevent, detect and respond effectively to future public health threats.

articles.content: United says it won’t let personal AI assistants book tickets on the airline, citing both privacy and regulatory concerns. The company says it hasn’t yet seen many people try to use AI agents to book their flights, The Wall Street Journal reports, in line with observations from other businesses like Doordash. But United is concerned that agents could expose customers’ information or make purchases they didn’t intend, and potentially skirt federal rules about the kind of information airlines need to share with customers — like having them attest that their bags don’t have explosives. While agents can still show users United flights, they won’t be able to actually complete the transaction on their behalf. The decision, and others like it, could limit the potential usefulness of newer personal AI assistants like Meta’s Muse and OpenAI’s Dots. “To be honest, I don’t want to create another middleman,” United CEO Scott Kirby said at an event on Tuesday, according to the Journal. Across sectors, businesses are grappling with whether to let AI agents transact on their sites, and United is not alone in blocking access for unauthorized agents. eBay appeared to block agents from browsing the site, and several major banks have also placed restrictions on them. United suggests it could reconsider its decision based on future advancements. “As third-party AI agents advance, we see the opportunities they present. However, at the same time, allowing them to interact directly with a United account or booking could involve sensitive actions, and we want to make sure we have established protections for travelers first.”

articles.title: Trump says the towering arch he wants to build might be dedicated to military veterans
articles.description: Trump says the towering arch he wants to build might be dedicated to military veterans AP News Trump Visits Arlington Cemetery as His Proposed Arch Faces Growing Opposition The New York Times Kennedys sue to block Trump’s gilded arch, saying it would ‘cast shadow’ over JFK gravesite The Guardian Trump wants to arm his DC arch. Experts see a threat. Politico Kennedy family members join legal fight over Trump’s arch Th
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump observed Veterans Day by suggesting that the towering arch he wants to build in his own honor would also be dedicated to the U.S. military and those who served in its ranks. That’s despite three veterans having sued to stop the project — which a federal court has since temporarily blocked. Some military groups have cheered the arch, but many others have opposed it or joined efforts to stop construction. Trump has said for months that the 250-foot (76-meter) arch set for construction near Arlington National Cemetery and the Lincoln Memorial would be inspired by the Arc de Triomphe in Paris, and might even be called the “Arc de Trump.” Washington commuters drive South over the Memorial Bridge that spans the Potomac River toward a traffic circle at the entrance of Arlington National Cemetery, the proposed site for President Donald Trump’s Triumphal Arch, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026, as seen from the Washington Monument. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite) Washington commuters drive South over the Memorial Bridge that spans the Potomac River toward a traffic circle at the entrance of Arlington National Cemetery, the proposed site for President Donald Trump’s Triumphal Arch, Friday, Nov. 6, 2026, as seen from the Washington Monument. (AP Photo/J. Scott Applewhite) He’s also insisted that Washington has wanted a similar structure for centuries — even though that’s not true. In comments during an annual ceremony at Arlington Cemetery on Wednesday, however, Trump suggested it was actually veterans who had longed for an arch in the capital. “And soon we’re going to dedicate a magnificent triumphal arc to our veterans,” he said. “And that’s in honor of our great veterans and our great militaries.” He added: “They’ve been waiting for it for 200 years.” Though the arch received approval from oversight boards stacked with members chosen by Trump, the three veterans are among several entities suing to block the arch’s construction. Nine family members of the Kennedy political dynasty are also seeking to stop the project, arguing that the arch would cast a shadow over their relatives’ gravesites at Arlington National Cemetery. A protest structure stands near Memorial Circle, the proposed site for a Triumphal Arch, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, in Arlington, Va. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) A protest structure stands near Memorial Circle, the proposed site for a Triumphal Arch, Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, in Arlington, Va. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) Last week, U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a temporary restraining order, prohibiting work for 14 days. With Democrats soon taking control of Congress after big wins all over the country in last week’s midterm elections, Trump’s renovation projects will encounter far more scrutiny and roadblocks — from his effort to put his own name on the Kennedy Center to remaking a public golf course and building his massive White House ballroom and the arch. Despite the midterm defeats by his party and the potential legal and legislative hurdles, the White House has continued to promote the arch project. President Donald Trump speaks during an event to mark Veterans Day at Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Va., Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein) President Donald Trump speaks during an event to mark Veterans Day at Arlington National Cemetery in Arlington, Va., Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (AP Photo/Mark Schiefelbein) That includes a slick website unveiled last week which proclaimed that it’d be known as the United States Military Triumphal Arch and was “long overdue, and has been sought for many years, especially by the Military.” The website prominently displays a picture of and quote from Trump. It also features the word “Triumph” in gold cursive script recalling the typeface used at the president’s Mar-a-Lago estate in Florida and similar flourishes that have been affixed to the White House as part of his overhaul of the Oval Office and West Wing. The arch’s plans call for its columns to store munitions and areas on the pedestal and observation deck to be set aside for a sniper’s nest. Its base would be designed to launch drones, and the site says that the overall monument “will be Highly Secretive but, at the same time, a Top Level and Lethal structure, the likes of which has not been seen in this Country before.” The website does not say how much the project will cost or how it will be paid for, although some estimates have reached as high as $100 million.
