A New Way of Seeing the Universe: MSU’s Contribution to Nobel-Winning Neutrino Research
articles.description: Michigan State University has been involved in the IceCube Neutrino Observatory for about 12 years, contributing to an international scientific project based at the South Pole that studies subatomic particles […]
articles.content: Michigan State University has been involved in the IceCube Neutrino Observatory for about 12 years, contributing to an international scientific project based at the South Pole that studies subatomic particles originating from some of the universe’s most energetic phenomena with the goal of solving some of the universe’s most challenging problems. A team of students, researchers, and engineers at MSU are part of the international IceCube project, led by researcher Francis Halzen, who in early October received the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics, awarded by the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences, “for his decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin.” Alejandra Granados, a Salvadorian graduate student specializing in particle astrophysics, worked on the installation of hardware in the optical modules as part of the IceCube Upgrade. Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz for City Pulse A “cute idea,” as Halzen described it on a phone call after learning about the Nobel Prize, emerged in the late 1980s, when he envisioned a way to capture traces of an invisible fundamental particle called a neutrino using a new type of telescope: IceCube. “We weren’t shocked”, said Tyce DeYoung, a professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy and head of the MSU IceCube research group. “But it was certainly exciting. We’ve thought the science behind has been exciting for a very long time, and we wanted to see Francis recognized; he’s been clearly the moving force behind this project since the very beginning.” “But, as Francis has said several times,” DeYoung said, “he views this as a prize for all of us for this work that we’ve done together. And so that was very exciting. I am very proud of him, but also, we’re very proud too of the contributions we’ve made.” The Nobel announcement surprised both outsiders and project insiders. Tyce DeYoung, a professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy and head of the MSU IceCube research group. Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz for City Pulse “I was very excited to see him win because particle physics hasn’t won a Nobel in 10 years,” said Alejandra Granados-Hernández, a graduate student specializing in particle astrophysics and part of the hardware production for the IceCube Upgrade, a new part of the project in which the MSU team participated by improving sensor calibrations last year. “And when I literally woke up, I saw that one of my professors had posted that Halzen had been awarded the Nobel, and there were tons of people celebrating and congratulating him. So it was super cool, because it felt like finally receiving recognition.” And this recognition has drawn public attention to the scientists involved and put the project in the spotlight, as it “wasn’t valued or understood enough,” said Dan Salazar-Gallegos, an MSU Physics post-doc who worked as lead physicist in the IceCube upgrade. “Without a doubt, the Nobel Prize has made it much more popular than it was just a few weeks ago, so it’s fantastic to hear from people who had never heard of it before.” The project resulted from international scientific cooperation involving 14 countries and 400 scientists. It cost $279 million, and the United States funded a large portion of the project, although IceCube avoided a proposed 50% budget cut pushed by President Donald Trump’s administration earlier this year. Congress rejected the drastic budget slash and secured five more years of funding for the IceCube. But what are neutrinos, why the IceCube, and why Antarctica? “They’re incredibly unique particles,” Salazar-Gallegos said, of neutrinos. “People may have heard them called ‘ghost particles’ because, for the most part, they pass through virtually everything. That’s why it takes such a large telescope to detect them. We receive tens of millions of them every day. They interact very rarely, but over many years, it becomes possible to start reconstructing where they came from.” DeYoung said scientists believe some of the universe’s most powerful particle accelerators may be located near supermassive black holes, where particles are accelerated to energies roughly 100 million times greater than those achieved by the most powerful accelerators on Earth, including CERN. Digital optical modules, or mDOMS, built at MSU as part of the IceCube upgrade. Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz for City Pulse Despite more than a century of research into these cosmic phenomena, their origins and mechanisms remain largely unknown. By detecting neutrinos, there is hope to gain new insights into these extreme environments and better understand the powerful processes shaping the universe. And here is where the IceCube Observatory plays its key part. “Galileo Galilei invented the first optical telescope,” DeYoung said. “And we learned many things from that. In the 20th century, many new types of telescopes were developed: radio telescopes, infrared telescopes, gamma-ray telescopes, and every new way that we find to look at the universe, we discover amazing things that we hadn’t thought about, we hadn’t understood. IceCube is the latest.” “It’s another new way of looking at the universe,” he said. “And it tells us about things that we don’t see very well in optical astronomy or in X-ray or radio astronomy.” About 3 kilometers under the Antarctic ice, beneath billions of tons of ice, IceCube consists of rows of more than 5,000 digital optical modules and was constructed between 2004 and 2011. The 5,000 detectors, each slightly larger than a soccer ball, together make a giant cube, nearly a kilometer wide. MSU physics lab equipment. Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz for City Pulse And they make it possible to detect the traces left by neutrinos. “Going to Vancouver or Hawaii would be a lot more convenient than going to the South Pole,” DeYoung said. “It would certainly be a lot more pleasant to conduct an experiment, but it turns out that the engineering that you need in the deep ocean is much more difficult than it is at the South Pole.” This is one of the few things that’s easier to do in Antarctica than anywhere else on Earth. “It’s easier,” DeYoung adds. “Because it’s not under the water, and it’s easier because the South Pole ice is freshwater, so it’s not corrosive like saltwater is. Once it freezes, it stops trying to destroy our equipment.” MSU and the IceCube Before IceCube, there was AMANDA (Antarctic Muon and Neutrino Detector Array), a precursor detector that advanced neutrino research in Antarctica. DeYoung said his doctoral thesis focused on demonstrating that AMANDA could identify neutrinos, laying some of the scientific groundwork for the development of observatories like IceCube. Involvement began through individuals, not an institution. DeYoung started about 30 years ago as a graduate student at the University of Wisconsin, working within Francis Halzen’s group; his colleague Nathan Whitehorn joined about 15 years later. Both eventually became faculty members and brought the work to MSU. Emmett Krupczak, a National Science Foundation graduate research fellow, and project lead for the IceCube upgrade construction project at MSU. Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz for City Pulse “The university was very enthusiastic about the science we were conducting. In fact, we now have several faculty members who have been involved,” DeYoung said. “So, MSU has been involved for about 12 years and has been a major supporter.” One of MSU’s most significant institutional contributions was its participation in the IceCube Upgrade project, an initiative to enhance the observatory’s calibration and measurement capabilities. Last year, 400 more sensitive modules were installed inside the ice. Of these new modules, MSU assembled 205 as part of the IceCube Upgrade project, developed through a collaboration between Michigan State University, the University of Wisconsin, and scientific partners in Germany and Japan. The sensors were assembled at MSU’s Biomedical and Physical Sciences Building in East Lansing, with production beginning in spring 2024. The project also provided students, around 18 undergrads, with an opportunity to participate directly in an international scientific collaboration, contributing to the manufacturing, testing, quality control and calibration of the equipment. According to the university, the new modules are designed to be two to three times more sensitive than the existing optical sensors. Emmett Krupczak, a National Science Foundation Graduate Research Fellow and project lead for the IceCube Upgrade’s construction, traveled to the South Pole from early November 2025 through February 2026 to participate in the installation process. “It was extremely exciting to see modules that we built right here at MSU travel all the way down to the South Pole,” Krupczak said. “The holes for the modules go about 2.5 kilometers down into the ice, so drilling them is a project in itself! I really appreciated having the opportunity to work on both the drilling side and the module installation side, because I got to participate in the whole process of constructing the detector, starting from parts in the lab and finishing with a fully tested module more than 2 kilometers deep in the ice.” The project will not be limited to a single location for observing the universe. Although IceCube is the first operational telescope of its kind, researchers say its ability to pinpoint neutrino origins remains limited. Its relatively low angular resolution provides only a broad picture of the sky, leaving many questions about the universe’s most energetic phenomena unanswered. MSU physics lab equipment. Photo by Erick Díaz Veliz for City Pulse “The IceCube is the first telescope of this type that works,” DeYoung said. “And it’s starting to tell us very interesting things, but it has kind of a little bit of a fuzzy or foggy view of the sky. It doesn’t have the precision. If we go to a radio astronomer and tell them what our angular resolution is, they kind of laugh at us because they’re like, ‘Well, that’s cute.’ So it’s the first step.” To address these limitations, several MSU researchers are working on the Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment (P-ONE), a proposed next-generation neutrino observatory designed to provide greater precision and a sharper view of the universe. Located in the Northern Hemisphere, the instrument would also offer a better vantage point for studying the Milky Way, which IceCube cannot observe as effectively from its position at the South Pole. After the Nobel Prize, team members are more encouraged than ever to continue their research and explore how far this new field of astronomy can take them in their own professional careers. Looking back to before completing his doctorate, Granados-Hernández had hoped to help develop new methods for searching for neutrino sources that utilize machine learning. Afterward, she intends to continue researching neutrinos and to remain involved in mentoring, as she has done since her first year, to help others envision themselves in a scientific career. Salazar-Gallegos hopes to keep researching dark matter and join a team that says something definitive, or at least interesting, about it. “We’re at a point in our history where we can break patterns and establish new standards for ourselves,” Salazar-Gallegos added. “And all those barriers that existed, and still exist, can be broken down in ways that weren’t possible before.”

articles.title: 'Policing Passengers': how Black women turned bus rides into a fight for citizenship
articles.description: In her new book, Eastern Michigan University Professor Mary-Elizabeth Murphy chronicles how bus companies treated Black women traveling across state lines as second-class citizens.
articles.content: Eastern Michigan University professor, Mary-Elizabeth Murphy, is the author of new book, "Policing Passengers: Black Women and the Fight Against Bus Violence". (Kalloli Bhatt / Michigan Public)Michigan history rightly celebrates late Detroiter Rosa Parks as the woman who took on the burden of the Montgomery bus boycott by refusing to give up her bus seat during the Jim Crow Era. But she was not the first or the only one. During World War II — as the country began to mass produce military hardware and supplies on a a scale not seen before — hundreds of thousands of Black American women found jobs, that for some required them to travel out of the state and for others provided economic opportunities to be able to travel on their own across state lines for the first time. Speaking with Stateside host April Baer, Eastern Michigan University history professor Mary-Elizabeth Murphy discussed her new book, "Policing Passengers: Black Women and the Fight Against Bus Violence." Her book tells the stories of women who faced intense physical violence and harassment from bus companies, including Greyhound, while traveling across state lines. There were two types of buses that existed in the American transportation landscape at the time, explained Murphy. The two types were city buses and interstate buses. Mary-Elizabeth Murphy is a Professor of History at Eastern Michigan University(Courtesy / Eastern Michigan University)"Black women often rode interstate buses when they were visiting friends or family, especially in the eras of war and the Great Migration," she said. While it was a small percentage of the population of working women during this industrial boom, Murphy said, for many Black women these jobs positioned them as key members of the industrial labor force of the time. Despite Black women becoming some of the most consistent riders of interstate buses, bus companies did not want Black women as passengers."Black women were some for the most consistent riders and they would trade passenger stories, and they quickly learned the etiquette of bus segregation," Murphy said.Some women, she said, faced physical beatings while ridings and others were even banned from using restrooms and restaurants at rest stops.Between the 1920s and 1940s, African American women filed dozens of lawsuits against bus companies, like the case of Paulina Stevens from Detroit. In 1929, Stevens, a 36-year old migrant from Georgia, was living in an interracial marriage in Black Bottom in Detroit when she boarded a Greyhound bus to travel to Lima, Ohio. "On the way back, she was put in the very back of the bus and rain poured (on) it and soaked her clothes," Murphy said. "So by the time she arrived in Detroit, she was ill." Stevens had very little formal education, but she knew that as a Michigander, she was protected by a civil rights statue — prompting her to sue Greyhound. "Her case went to Detroit, and a judge awarded her $100 in damages, but then Greyhound appealed the case and it traveled to a district court in Ann Arbor," Murphy said. It was there that Washtenaw County Circuit Court Judge George Washington Samples ruled in favor of Stevens and called out Greyhound over its discriminatory practices against African Americans. "He was terrified that if states like Michigan didn't step into prevent discrimination on the part of these bus companies that African Americans would revolt," Murphy added. "So he increased her [Stevens'] award by $250, which in today's money is about $4,000 dollars." It was Stevens' lawsuit that set a precedent for Detroit resident Lois Wright to become a bus driver — nearly two decades later — when the bus industry was hit hard by the crisis of World War II."Because there are so many wartime jobs, there aren't enough workers to drive city buses in Detroit — and so in early 1943, newspapers report that there are over 200 buses that are sitting idle in parking lots in Detroit because there are no workers to drive them, because bus driving is a white man's job," Murphy said.Eventually, the need forced Detroit to relent and hire Wright, who became the first Black woman bus driver in the United States.It was not until 1946 that the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that racial segregation on interstate commerce posed an undue burden. Full interview with author Mary-Elizabeth MurphyApril Baer: This is Stateside. I'm April Baer. Michigan history rightly celebrates late-life Detroiter Rosa Parks as the woman who took on the burden of the Montgomery bus boycott, becoming an icon of the civil rights movement in the process.But Rosa Parks is not the only story. A professor at Eastern Michigan University has written a new book highlighting the histories of women riding to work, family and opportunity, and what happened to them along the way. The book is called, "Policing Passengers: Black Women and the Fight Against Bus Violence." The author is my guest, Professor Murphy, who teaches history, philosophy and women's and gender studies at Eastern Michigan University in Ypsilanti. Mary-Elizabeth, welcome to Stateside.Murphy: Thank you so much for having me.Baer: You write that before Rosa, there was Rosie the Riveter. Can you lay some groundwork for us about how the wartime industrial economy was a pivotal place for the kind of battles you wanted to write about?Murphy: During World War II, about 600,000 African American women were able to obtain wartime jobs. Even though this was a small percentage, it was a game changer because, for the first time, Black women had labor that tied them to the state. My book chronicles how Black women used bus rides to press for full citizenship rights in the United States. The Rosie I talk about is Irene Morgan, who was a war worker in Baltimore. She labored at an aircraft plant.Baer: This was a whole other piece of history that I was unaware of — the fact that there was interstate work during the years when women were taking a bigger role in industrial labor.Murphy: Absolutely. There were two types of buses in the American transportation landscape at this point: city buses, like the one Rosa Parks rode, and interstate buses. Black women often rode interstate buses when visiting friends or family, especially during wartime and the Great Migration.In 1944, Irene Morgan was visiting her mother in Gloucester County, Virginia. After a restorative stay, she needed to return to Baltimore for her job at the aircraft plant. While riding a Greyhound bus, she sat in a designated seat for African Americans. But because buses were overcrowded during World War II, the driver ordered her to move. She refused and was arrested.She contested her case, which went to the Supreme Court of Virginia, where it was rejected. The U.S. Supreme Court later agreed to hear the case and, in 1946, ruled that racial segregation in interstate commerce posed an undue burden.Baer: Irene Morgan's case going to the Supreme Court seems like a major moment in civil rights and transportation law. Why have most schoolchildren never heard of her, while so many people visit the Henry Ford and see the bus Rosa Parks rode?Murphy: I think there are two big issues. First, the Morgan case, while very important, was not enforced. That's why African Americans had to continue fighting bus segregation and stage the Freedom Rides. They also had a Ride of Reconciliation to test enforcement. Even though the law was on their side, Southern states refused to follow it.The second issue is that the Montgomery bus boycott ended in victory, signaling that segregation on city buses was over. As you pointed out, there is a difference between city and interstate buses.Baer: I'd like to talk more about that. Interstate bus service is something low-income people still rely on for long-distance trips. Did you find evidence of what bus companies thought about Black women as a target market in the early days of interstate bus service?Murphy: Bus companies did not want Black women passengers. My research demonstrated that bus companies, particularly Greyhound, based their bus drivers on police officers. They drew on military and police practices to instruct drivers to police Black women passengers.Baer: I can't unsee that now that I've seen some of the diagrams and other information you shared in the book.Murphy: It's stunning to see how law enforcement was the model. But it makes sense because enforcing racial segregation on a bus was difficult. It's such a cramped space, and the driver had to wield authority like a police officer.Even though thousands of African American women traveled on interstate buses during this period — whether as part of the Great Migration, to visit friends and family, advance their education or attend conventions — the bus industry tried to dissuade them from riding.They were segregated and put in the back of the bus, whether in the North or South. They were also banned from vehicles altogether. Bus drivers used their uniforms and accessories, including guns, billy clubs and ticket punchers, to assault and harass Black women passengers.Baer: The literature of the period from within the transportation industry was also wildly racist, with caricatures in illustrations that are eye-popping today. How did you find all this archived magazine material and industry trade publications?Murphy: I traveled to two major archives in Chicago and Cleveland to investigate the Greyhound bus company papers. In Chicago, I made two discoveries. First, Greyhound hired its head of bus drivers from the New York City Police Department. In 1929, the company appointed Marcus Dow, who had spent years in the department learning racial policing. They made him the model for all bus drivers.The archive only had a few boxes, and archivists warned me I wouldn't find anything. But I found gold. Greyhound and other bus companies offered an in-bus magazine, similar to the passenger magazines available on airplanes today. There were only a few issues, but they were crucial. They demonstrated that Greyhound and other bus companies wanted to other passengers of color, first on the page and then on the bus.After finding fragments of those periodicals, I went to the Library of Congress and read every travel issue Greyhound had circulated. This helped me understand how the company constructed violent and racist mythologies about Black passengers, as well as Indigenous passengers, Mexican passengers and other immigrants.Baer: Black women did become customers of Greyhound and other transportation providers. You write about a woman named Irene Davis, who in 1931 purchased a round-trip bus ticket to visit her family. Can you talk about how her trip went sideways?Murphy: Irene Davis was a resident of Philadelphia, and in 1931, she purchased a Greyhound bus ticket to travel home for Christmas. This was common during the Great Migration, when African American women traveled during the holidays or summer to visit family.The bus trip down was uneventful, but on the way back, she discovered that she and five other Black passengers had been put in the very back of the bus, sharing a crowded seat. She noticed that the driver was rough and violent with her. She also discovered that African American women were banned from restrooms and restaurants at rest stops.She said she had seen Greyhound advertisements and thought it was a company that valued customer service, but she was about to change her opinion.Baer: She was identified on the bus as an aggressive or problem passenger.Murphy: Yes, absolutely.Baer: She was singled out by the driver. What ended up happening on her trip?Murphy: She was so upset by her mistreatment that, when she returned home to Philadelphia, she wrote two letters. First, she wrote to Greyhound, saying she was a paying customer who had spent her hard-earned money on a ticket and was incredibly dissatisfied.She also wrote to the NAACP, describing her experiences and the driver's violence. This showed the NAACP that hundreds of African Ameri

Election denialism losing steam as Trump flip flops on accepting midterm results
articles.description: The day after Democrats won sweeping victories in the midterm elections, an Arizona county official delivered a stark warning to his fellow Republicans about election denialism — it needed to stop. The state has been a hotbed of election fraud conspiracy theories. After President Donald Trump’s 2020 election loss, state lawmakers even pursued an audit […]
articles.content: President Donald Trump speaks in the White House briefing room on Nov. 9, 2026. (Photo by Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)The day after Democrats won sweeping victories in the midterm elections, an Arizona county official delivered a stark warning to his fellow Republicans about election denialism — it needed to stop. The state has been a hotbed of election fraud conspiracy theories. After President Donald Trump’s 2020 election loss, state lawmakers even pursued an audit in Maricopa County, which includes Phoenix, that found no evidence of fraud. “To my fellow Republicans who have been trafficking in these lies for the last six years, you need to stop,” Maricopa County Supervisor Thomas Galvin said at a county Board of Supervisors meeting. As Republicans grasp for answers following their stunning losses, election officials, voting rights advocates and researchers are watching to see whether Trump will lead the party toward false narratives around election fraud or to accept normal explanations, such as voter dissatisfaction and poor campaign messages. The path they choose could help determine whether the country moves past an era defined by Trump’s election denial after his 2020 loss. But Trump has sent mixed signals. As the scale of GOP losses became clear last week, Trump initially pledged to accept the results. That changed over the weekend. On Truth Social, Trump shared posts from others suspicious of the results. By Monday, he had grown more explicit. “Does anybody really believe that this ‘Election’ was honest. How could the Polls be so wrong???” Trump wrote in a social media post. ‘180 in an hour’ Polls leading up to the midterms largely favored Democrats, though some understated the level of support for Democratic candidates. Trump has long promoted falsehoods about stolen elections and voter fraud. After the 2016 election, Trump claimed millions of people had illegally voted for Democrat Hillary Clinton. In 2020, Trump tried to overturn his losses in key battleground states with lawsuits that raised unfounded claims of fraud. His rhetoric eventually led his supporters to storm the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021. Pro-Trump protesters gather in front of the U.S. Capitol on Jan. 6, 2021 before storming the building and clashing with police officers. (Photo by Jon Cherry/Getty Images) He also pressured election officials, including a demand that Georgia Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger “find” enough votes to overturn his loss in the state. Gabriel Sterling, a Republican and former longtime official in the Georgia Secretary of State’s Office, publicly denounced Trump’s allegations of voter fraud in the wake of the 2020 election. Now a senior fellow at the Secure Democracy Foundation, a nonprofit focused on strengthening elections, Sterling voiced concern this week that election denialism will become a tactic of politicians moving forward. “I was sort of surprised and pleased about the president’s initial responses,” Sterling said in an interview. “But I also took it with a grain of salt, knowing that he can go 180 in an hour, depending on who he’s talking to.” Fewer online rumors Election rumors haven’t gained nearly the same level of traction this year as they did in 2020, researchers of online disinformation say. Immediately after Trump’s initial acknowledgment of Republican defeat, only a few committed election denialists were questioning not simply the results but the security of the elections, according to The Election Rumor Rundown, a website by the Center for an Informed Public at the University of Washington. Kate Starbird, a professor at the University of Washington who studies online disinformation, wrote in a viral social media post last week that the atmosphere in her lab was “giddy” as her team absorbed the possibility that claims of rigged elections may be in the past, “at least for the time being.” As Trump has moved back toward denialism, however, online conversation around denialism and conspiracy theories has grown. Starbird shared a graph on Monday showing a spike in discussions on X focused on rigged, dishonest or fraudulent elections after Trump posted on his site, Truth Social. In a Monday interview, Starbird said “hardcore” election deniers have been advancing conspiracy theories for the past week. They have been excited by Trump’s return to the denialism conversation, which she said also drew in additional online influencers. Still, Starbird said election deniers lack the kind of popular support and infrastructure they’ve enjoyed in the past. Within days of Election Day 2020, protests were already emerging around the results, but that kind of on-the-ground movement is absent this year. “I’m still pretty confident that the ingredients for a full-fledged election denialism movement are not in place,” Starbird said. Lawsuits show ‘red line’ Since Election Day, conspiracy theories have not received nearly as much attention from major media platforms as they did following the 2020 election. That year, Trump supporters made wild, false claims about voting machines during TV appearances. Some of those statements led to massive legal payouts. Dominion Voting Systems, a large manufacturer of election equipment, sued Fox News, alleging defamation by hosts and guests. Fox settled the lawsuit in 2023 for $787.5 million. In 2024, Newsmax settled a lawsuit filed by Smartmatic, which builds electronic voting systems, for $40 million. Two former Georgia election workers sued former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani, a Trump political adviser, for defamation surrounding the 2020 election, and secured a $148 million judgment against him. In early 2025, the women reached a settlement that included undisclosed compensation. “I think those suits did chastise people and remind potential dangerous elements where the red line is where you can really get yourself in trouble,” Kevin Johnson, executive director of Election Reformers Network, a nonpartisan group that seeks to protect elections from polarization, said in an interview. Election deniers join administration At the same time, Johnson added, some election deniers ended up working in the second Trump administration. Then-Attorney General Pam Bondi listens as President Donald Trump speaks in the East Room of the White House on March 16, 2026. (Photo by Alex Wong/Getty Images) Former U.S. Attorney General Pam Bondi said Trump had won Pennsylvania in 2020, though Biden won. FBI Director Kash Patel has refused to say whether Biden won the 2020 election — a stance echoed by numerous Trump nominees who evade offering a direct answer when questioned during congressional hearings. Since Election Day, some Trump supporters have joined the president in embracing denialism about the midterms. Kari Lake, a prominent Arizona Republican and Trump’s nominee to be U.S. ambassador to Jamaica, wrote on social media without evidence that the “math isn’t mathing here.” Mike Lindell, the former MyPillow CEO, has called for a “full recount” of the midterm elections. However, nearly all high-ranking elected Republicans have acknowledged the losses, with some putting forward political and policy explanations. For instance, Vice President JD Vance, widely expected to run for president in 2028, faulted the war with Iran and hasn’t repeated Trump’s denialism comments. Sen. Ted Cruz, who will soon be the only Texas Republican in a statewide office, described the election results as a “Watergate-level repudiation.” House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, said the “people have spoken.” Confidence in elections Election denialism’s more limited reach so far this year among leading Republicans — other than Trump — comes after election administrators spent the past six years attempting to bolster public confidence in elections, current and former election officials said. Minnesota Secretary of State Steve Simon, a Democrat, said in an interview that election officials had prepared to respond to false claims surrounding the election, not only by rebutting falsehoods but also providing accurate information about elections and the results. In his state, that included going to court if the Trump administration attempted to interfere, he said. But so far, Simon said, the volume of rigged and stolen election claims in Minnesota doesn’t match what he’s seen before. “Compared to past election cycles, I have seen fewer examples after this election of people making election denialism claims,” Simon said. Americans broadly trust elections, according to a survey conducted in September and October by the Pew Research Center. Nearly identical percentages of registered voters supporting Republican and Democratic candidates — 90% and 91%, respectively — expressed some level of confidence that elections in their community would be well run. By contrast, 97% of Democratic-supporting voters voiced confidence in 2024, compared to 88% of Republican-supporting voters. Building trust in elections requires a lot of work in between elections, said Ari Mittleman, executive director of Keep Our Republic, a pro-democracy nonprofit. Over time, the role of election officials has evolved to encompass public outreach. “Even if their job description largely centers around being an administrator, they now need to be an ambassador for the entire profession,” Mittleman said in an interview. Ahead of Election Day, Trump and other federal officials declined to flatly rule out forms of federal election interference, raising fears among Democrats and voting rights advocates that the administration would try to disrupt voting or discredit the results. The Trump administration heavily promoted efforts to root out noncitizen voting. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security arrested dozens of noncitizens over alleged election crimes in the weeks before the election and the U.S. Department of Justice sued dozens of states in an unsuccessful attempt to obtain sensitive voter data to aid its efforts to find noncitizen voters. The Justice Department also sued California to try to force the state to set aside the ballots of 20,000 individuals the Trump administration said were suspected noncitizens. The DOJ dropped the lawsuit after the Supreme Court rejected the request on the eve of Election Day. Will ‘fever’ break? Speaking on the Friday after Election Day, Simon said he remained ready for legal action if necessary. He said he was pleasantly surprised by Trump’s tentative acceptance of the results, but warned that “as we’ve come to know and learn, that could change” — seeming to anticipate the president’s turn toward denialism days later. Simon said he was not yet convinced the 2026 election would “break the fever” of election denialism, given the looming presidential race in 2028. Election deniers are still incentivized to push false claims for online attention or money, he said. “My hope is that we can get back to understanding that elections are fundamentally fair and honest and secure,” Simon said.

articles.description: WASHINGTON — Democrats and business leaders publicly lobbied the Trump administration Wednesday to prioritize work permits and other protections for long-term immigrants during the lame-duck session of Congress and beyond. Citing the midterm elections, when Democrats flipped the U.S House and Senate, and President Donald Trump’s recent admission that his immigration crackdown hurt Republicans at […]
articles.content: U.S. Sen. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., speaks outside the U.S. Capitol during a press conference with business leaders to push for work protections for immigrants on Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026. (Photo by Ariana Figueroa/States Newsroom)WASHINGTON — Democrats and business leaders publicly lobbied the Trump administration Wednesday to prioritize work permits and other protections for long-term immigrants during the lame-duck session of Congress and beyond. Citing the midterm elections, when Democrats flipped the U.S House and Senate, and President Donald Trump’s recent admission that his immigration crackdown hurt Republicans at the ballot box, Democratic lawmakers argued that voters were clear about wanting immigration reform before the start of the next Congress. Congress has a lengthy to-do-list for the lame-duck session, possibly including government funding, the annual defense policy bill, the farm bill, a measure to regulate the college sports landscape and permitting reform to ease regulation on large construction projects. “We owe it to these families to try anything, and I’m willing to try anything,” Arizona Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego said. He was joined by American Business Immigration Coalition Action, which lobbies for work permits and legal pathways for long-term immigrants, and the South Texas Builders Association, a local trade group that represents the construction industry that has a workforce that is 30% immigrant nationwide, and Democratic U.S. House members from Texas. Asked how receptive the White House would be to work permits for immigrants, which the administration has vigorously worked to limit, Gallego didn’t directly answer. Trump’s mixed signals The administration has revoked millions of immigrants’ work permits in the last two years. Many were workers in hospitality, healthcare and the construction industries. But shortly after the midterm elections, the president said he was open to making a deal on work permits in certain industries. At the same time, though, he elevated Stephen Miller, an official who has crafted some of the president’s harshest immigration policies, to White House chief of staff. “I think right now the best thing the White House could do is to actually try to send some type of signal, besides talk, that they’re serious about this, and the way to do that is to have some reforms already at (Immigration and Customs Enforcement),” Gallego said. “Whether it’s shutting down the detention centers, giving (a) certain level of protections, whether to veterans so they don’t get deported, to maybe parents of U.S. students so they don’t get deported, something to show that it’s not just talk, and this isn’t going to be a policy that’s led by Stephen Miller,” he added. The vice chair of South Texas Builders Association, Benny Melendez, had a pointed message for Miller. “If you want to continue harassing our communities, prepare yourself not only to lose your job, but … these same communities you are now harassing will make sure you lose the White House” in 2028, he said. Next Congress If lawmakers are unable to get any major reforms through the crowded end-of-year session, Democrats are looking ahead to when they control both chambers next year. House Republicans on Tuesday elected Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, a staunch Trump supporter who has not supported immigration reform, to lead them in the minority. Texas Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar, the incoming chair on the subcommittee that handles government funding for the Department of Homeland Security, said he’s not worried about Jordan because Democrats will have a majority in January. Cuellar, whom Trump pardoned after he and his wife were indicted on charges of bribery, money laundering and conspiracy, said he’s going to use his subcommittee gavel to add guardrails on ICE and clear the backlog at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which processes legal immigrants. Gallego said he thinks the Senate will be able to get to 60 votes on some type of immigration reform legislation in the 120th Congress, when Democrats will have at least 54 and up to 56 seats depending on races that are still too close to call. Whether that overhaul is in one bill or a series of increments is up for debate, Gallego said. “If we can pass a big, beautiful conference immigration reform bill, the Trump immigration reform bill, and if that gets them on our side or not, then let’s do that,” Gallego said. “But if that doesn’t work, then I do think incremental passes to start protecting different communities I think is also an option. We should not avoid that either.”

articles.title: Blue-Nami ‘26: Fewer Split Tickets Turn Familiar Dem Margins Into Historic Gains
articles.description: The beating Democrats put on Republicans in Michigan last week can’t be gauged by the visible size of the bruise. It’s by how deep the bruise stretched beneath the skin. […]
articles.content: The beating Democrats put on Republicans in Michigan last week can’t be gauged by the visible size of the bruise. It’s by how deep the bruise stretched beneath the skin. Democrat Jocelyn Benson beat Republican John James on Nov. 3 by 10.85 percentage points. In 2022, Gretchen Whitmer beat Tudor Dixon by 10.53 percentage points. Abdul El-Sayed , Michigan Democratic candidate for the U.S. Senate, campaigns with Tiffany Muller, President of End Citizen’s United. Photo by Raymond Holt for City Pulse Democrat Abdul El-Sayed won his seat with 52.55% of the vote. Democratic U.S. Senate candidates, since 1936, have averaged 52.71% of the vote. It’s hard to call either result bigger. What made the 2026 “Blue-nami” so historic is how completely Democratic votes carried down ballot. Also, the traditional pendulum swing back to Republicans after a Democratic administration didn’t happen. “It was more than just a wave,” said Oakland University political science professor Dave Dulio. “The statewide and nationwide domination was consistent and widespread.” Jocelyn Benson. Photo by Lieza Klemm/City Pulse Let’s run through the numbers. – The Whitmer-Benson transition will be the first time a Democratic governor will hand off to a Democrat successor since 1961 and only the second time since the Republican Party started nominating candidates in 1854. – With El-Sayed’s election and assuming no early departures, Michigan will go 30 years without a Republican U.S. Senator, its longest-ever drought, which includes 1837-1854, when the GOP didn’t even exist. – Michigan Democrats picked up three congressional seats, reducing Michigan’s Republican congressional delegation to four starting in 2027, its lowest point since 1884 when Michigan had 11 members of Congress. – Democrats picked up three state Senate seats, creating a 23-15 majority, its largest margin since the end of 1982. – Democrats picked up 11 state House seats, its largest election pickup in 62 years. It will now have a 63-47 majority. – Only one of Michigan’s seven Supreme Court justices, Brian Zahra, was nominated by the Republican Party. Zahra is the only non-education post statewide Republican to win since 2018. A reason for these numbers is a nearly 20% jump in voters picking straight-ticket Democratic from 2022 to 2026. Republican straight ticket voting went up 16.7% during that same period. Lt. Governor Garlin Gilchrist, Democratic nominee for secretary of state at a Detroit rally on Oct. 24, 2026. Photo by Raymond Holt for City Pulse This widened the Democratic advantage in straight-ticket votes from 185,887 four years ago to 255,905 this year. Not as many voters are splitting their tickets. Competitive precincts in Downriver, Macomb County and elsewhere that split – a vote for Whitmer alongside a vote for a Republican state House candidate in 2018 and 2022 – are seeing more homogenized election results. Take Blackman Township in Jackson County, for example. In 2022, Republican Rep. Kathy Schmaltz (the former WILX anchor) won Blackman Township by 1,338 votes while Democrat Gretchen Whitmer won it by 160 votes. Mike Rogers, from his campaign website This year, Schmaltz won the Township by 179 votes. James won it by a nearly identical margin – 156 votes. That’s bad news for Republicans since Michigan, overall, tends to lean more Democratic than Republican. “Republicans could go from being a nearly extinct creature in 2027 to being a full extinct creature in 2029 if – and this is what I’m really concerned about – Michigan is not a battleground state in 2028,” said Republican political consultant Dennis Lennox. At the epicenter of it all is President Donald Trump. The war in Iran. The on-again, off-again tariffs strategy. The trade war with Canada. All of it came with gas hitting $5 a gallon. Grocery prices ballooned. High interest rates stifled the housing market. Friends Johnathan Whorton (left) and Sylvester McIntosh (right) reviewing election returns on television. “We’re seeing things we LOVE”. Photo by Raymond Holt for City Pulse Voters held the President responsible for the rising prices, and Republicans representing politically competitive districts paid the price this time, said Adrian Hemond of Grassroots Midwest. “When the numbers go, people get angry,” Hemond said. “As it turns out, when the President wrecks the economy on purpose and for political reasons, the voters will punish you for that.” Data centers, Flock cameras and the Muslim Brotherhood all came up as issues this campaign, but Hemond said all of these issues turned out to be “irrelevant.” Campaigns seemed to bring up issues “just to entertain each other,” because voters truly didn’t distinguish between the candidates. Republicans were pro-Trump. Democrats are not. They feel Trump is responsible for their current life situation. That’s all the information most voters needed to know. Attendees outside of a rally featuring President Donald Trump in Port Huron, Michigan, on Oct. 25, 2026 watch Trump speak on the screen outside of the event center. Photo by Lieza Klemm/City Pulse “Nobody gives a crap about what’s happening in Iran or how well the stock market is doing when they can’t afford groceries, they’re paying $5 for gas, and buying a home feels completely out of reach,” said Paul Cordes, the former Michigan Republican Party executive director. “It’s not rocket science. People didn’t suddenly become wonk Democrats overnight. “They voted to punish a party that promised to fight for working families, but hasn’t done nearly enough to make their lives better.” According to AdImpact, $172.8 million was spent on TV, streaming and internet ads trying to get Republican Mike Rogers elected to the U.S. Senate. By contrast, $108,856 was spent through those mediums to get Republican Tony Forlini elected secretary of state. Rogers lost with 45.45% of the vote. Forlini lost with 43.53% of the vote. “We saw very little crossover across office, across states, social groups or anything,” said Matt Grossmann, director of the Institute for Public Policy and Social Research. “People’s vote for state legislator was far more related to the President than their position on anything related to state government.” House Speaker Mike Johnson and U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett speak at the Ingham County Sheriff’s Office on Oct. 7, 2026. Mike Ellis/City Pulse Republican candidates were stuck. Speak in favor of Trump and lose a substantial segment of the population. Speak against Trump and potentially lose base support and possibly earn a primary opponent in the next election … if there is a next election for them. Incumbents in competitive districts, including U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett and U.S. Sen. Bill Huizenga, invited cabinet members and congressional leaders to town to talk about other issues where Team Trump could arguably claim successes. House Speaker Mike Johnson came to Michigan State’s Facility for Rare Isotope Beams (FRIB) with U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to highlight the $125 million Barrett helped bring to MSU to make it all happen. Johnson returned to Mason weeks later to highlight how much federal money Barrett scored for local law enforcement. Voters seemed to care about little beyond how life was becoming unaffordable. Former President Barack Obama and Michigan Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson stand before a capacity crowd at Cass Technical High School. Photo by Raymond Holt for City Pulse “If you’re raising a family of four on $90,000 a year, you’re screwed,” Hemond said. “A whole lot of people are not doing good right now. They’re cutting back where they can, but it’s not good.” Also, Trump has never won 50% of Michigan. He scored 47.5% in his 2016 victory and 49.73% in 2024. The point being that his allure was enough to win Michigan twice, but not much else. In the post-Rick Snyder era, Democratic candidates win with majorities in Michigan. Republicans do not. The numbers show neither party is doing much to expand the size of their universe. In the last three mid-term elections, the Democratic nominees for U.S. Senate, governor, secretary of state and attorney general have received all received between 55.86% and 49.04% of the vote, an average of 53.31%. The Republican nominees received between 46.26% and 41.93% of the vote, for an average of 44.11%. “Both parties are in a base-only posture right now,” Dulio said. “There’s little evidence to demonstrate that voters are interested in candidates who are from the other side. “They are pushing turnout models in these elections as opposed to persuasion models.” Turnout models are easier to execute, he said. It requires getting people out to the polls as opposed to the two-step process of convincing voters that you’re right and then getting them to vote, he said. If Michigan elections are destined for more strap-on-your-helmet-and-repeat cycle, Republicans would seem stuck in the mud. A Lawrence supporter reacts to Abdul El-Sayed’s announcement of victory in the Michigan senate race. Photo by Raymond Holt for City Pulse Could repeated Blue-namis become the anticipated norm as opposed to the exception? Cordes said he doesn’t believe it needs to be that way. The first step is connecting with a majority of voters. Talking and connecting with the guy working 60 hours a week trying to pay his mortgage, not the guy sitting in a boardroom “figuring out to squeeze another dollar out of him. The party needs to elevate candidates like Barrett, a married father of young kids, whose got a mortgage and is “a hell of a lot more concerned about what groceries cost than which hedge fund is going to outperform the market. “We need more leaders who actually live the same lives as the people we’re asking to vote Republicans,” Cordes said.

articles.title: White House faces unusual obstacle on confirming Trump judges: other Republicans
articles.content: WASHINGTON (AP) — Several Republican senators are complicating a White House plan to leave an enduring imprint on the judiciary long after President Donald Trump leaves office by throwing up obstacles for a handful of his judicial nominees in the final weeks of their Senate majority. In Texas, outgoing Sen. John Cornyn has expressed reservations about a top Justice Department official who has been nominated for a federal judgeship in the Dallas area. The two Arkansas senators, both Republicans, opposed a Trump nominee to a powerful appeals court seat, forcing the White House to withdraw Trump’s pick this week. And in Oklahoma, an appointed GOP senator has thrown up sudden objections to a district court nominee after earlier giving him the green light. Central to this effort are Cornyn and retiring North Carolina Sen. Thom Tillis, both of whom serve on the Judiciary Committee and are using their leverage to effectively block nominations on behalf of Republicans who aren’t on the panel. Though it comes after the midterm losses that weakened Trump’s political standing, this under-the-radar judiciary fight is more about Republicans asserting their powers over the administration’s judge selections, which has long been a cherished prerogative for senators, particularly for their home states. Asked about his opposition to the Arkansas and Oklahoma nominees, Tillis said he wants senators and their views on the prospective judges to be heard by the administration. His message to the White House, Tillis said, was: “Don’t treat us like a manufacturing facility. Treat us like the U.S. Senate.” “I’m not making a judgment about the merit of the nominee. I’m calling a foul on a process,” Tillis said in an interview with the Associated Press. “And the sooner the White House gets that, the more productive this next two years will be. If they don’t, they do so at their own peril.” Trump had nominated Lee Rudofsky of Arkansas to the 8th Circuit Court of Appeals. But the White House abruptly pulled that nomination on Tuesday, after Cornyn and Tillis had privately conveyed to Senate Judiciary Committee Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, that they would vote against Rudofsky in committee, according to two people with knowledge of the discussions who spoke on condition of anonymity to confirm private deliberations. Grassley also was forced to postpone a key committee vote on Tuesday for Oklahoma judicial nominee Zachary West because of opposition from Tillis on behalf of Sen. Alan Armstrong, one of the people said. The obstacles for the White House come as Senate Republicans have been racing to try to fill all remaining judicial vacancies this year, since they believe the new Democratic majority will have no interest in confirming Trump judges for lifetime appointments. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., told the AP last week that Democrats will not fill the bench with “crappy nominees,” and Grassley has pulled together an ambitious and aggressive confirmation timetable, much to the frustration of Democratic senators. Some of the nominations had been pending before the Nov. 3 midterms, which saw Republicans lose both the House and the Senate. But at least one judiciary vacancy in Texas is clearly being fast-tracked in a post-election rush. Elliot Gaiser, who leads the Justice Department’s Office of Legal Counsel, was first contacted by Texas Sen. Ted Cruz’s staff about becoming a federal judge on Nov. 4, the day after the election, according to his nominee questionnaire sent to the Senate Judiciary Committee. He has not been vetted by a bipartisan federal judicial evaluation committee that is traditionally used in Texas, Cornyn said. “Trying to air-drop somebody else in at the last minute for the Dallas vacancy that hasn’t been through that process, I think, is a concern,” Cornyn told the AP. Cornyn also noted Gaiser’s ties to efforts to overturn the 2020 election results that culminated in the Jan. 6, 2021, insurrection at the Capitol. Gaiser, then a lawyer for Trump’s reelection bid, was at the time advising the campaign on its election challenges, according to testimony given to the Jan. 6 select congressional committee. “I think there’s a better choice through some of the other nominees that have been thoroughly vetted and are available to serve,” Cornyn continued. “I certainly want to see us fill the seat.” Meanwhile, neither John Boozman nor Tom Cotton, the two Arkansas senators, had signed off on the appeals court nomination for Rudofsky, who currently holds a federal district court seat. Current Senate practice is that home-state consent isn’t necessary for nominees to the appeals courts, which span multiple states, although it is rare that a White House pursues any judge that isn’t supported by home-state senators from the same political party. Boozman and Cotton were thought to have been supportive of another candidate, Arkansas Supreme Court associate justice Cody Hiland. The justice said in August remarks at the University of Arkansas at Little Rock that he had interviewed specifically for the appeals court vacancy and went through an extensive vetting process by the FBI, but was eventually told by the White House counsel’s office that he was going to be nominated for a lower, district court position. Hiland said in his August speech to the law school that he declined the offer. In a brief interview, Boozman said simply that “we talked with other people that were certainly as capable.” Cotton declined to comment when approached in the Capitol. The White House did not return a request for comment on why it withdrew Rudofsky’s nomination, although Hiland was nominated at the same time. “The idea that you’re just going to roll over — that (the) White House has rolled over two senators from that state — obviously, other senators can see that happening to them if they sit and watch it happen,” Cornyn said of Rudofsky in an interview before his nomination was pulled by the White House. “So, I think there’ll be a lot of sympathy for the position of the two Arkansas senators.” The opposition to Oklahoma nominee Zachary West — a former counsel to Cruz in the Senate who currently serves in the Oklahoma attorney general’s office — may be temporary. Sen. Alan Armstrong had initially approved of the pick, but recently reversed course and privately conveyed his opposition to the nomination to other senators, according to two people with knowledge of the talks. Armstrong himself, though, is not in Washington for long. He had been appointed to replace Sen. Markwayne Mullin when he became Homeland Security secretary. Newly elected Oklahoma senator Kevin Hern is scheduled to be sworn in on Nov. 30. Armstrong said on Wednesday that his objections to West were “just purely qualification, versus the other candidates that we’ve suggested” and said the White House “basically ignored” other recommended candidates for the vacancy. As of Wednesday, there were 24 judicial nominations from Trump pending confirmation in the Senate, according to Grassley’s committee. So far under the president’s second term, the Senate has confirmed 57 judges, which include 10 appeals court judges, 46 district judges and one member of the Court of International Trade. Under Grassley, the Judiciary Committee has moved at what it said was the fastest pace since the Reagan administration. In a Wall Street Journal opinion piece published Tuesday, Grassley urged the Senate to confirm as many of the remaining judicial nominees as possible, writing: “The stakes are far too high for Republicans to take their feet off the gas now.” Outgoing Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., has conveyed similar sentiments. Cornyn and Tillis say they share that goal, but that protecting senatorial prerogative on judges was also important. Asked whether he was concerned he would anger the White House or Senate leadership with the tactics, Tillis responded: “I couldn’t care less.” Associated Press writer Mary Clare Jalonick contributed.

articles.title: T-Mobile illegally imposed 50GB cap on low-income home Internet plan, NY says
articles.description: Law requires 25Mbps home Internet. T-Mobile lowers speed to 600Kbps after 50GB cap.
articles.content: T-Mobile violated a New York state law by imposing a 50GB-per-month data cap and reducing speeds to less than a megabit per second on home Internet plans it is required to offer people with low incomes, New York government officials alleged. T-Mobile agreed to a settlement requiring it to scrap the data and speed limits, to offer the required low-income plans to more parts of the state, and to make it easier for customers to find information about the plans. The settlement requires T-Mobile to eliminate the speed limits and expand availability of the plans within 120 days. The alleged legal violation and the settlement are related to T-Mobile's wireless home Internet service, not the company's mobile plans. Governor Kathy Hochul and New York Attorney General Letitia James announced the settlement on Monday, saying that a state investigation found T-Mobile violated the New York Affordable Broadband Act (ABA).Read full article Comments

articles.title: Anduril says its first satellite can see adversaries maneuver in orbital night
articles.description: "What's unique is it's got a huge dynamic range. We can see things in full dark."
articles.content: Anduril Industries has announced the successful demonstration of a new satellite-based sensor designed to track other spacecraft that may be hiding their maneuvers in Earth's shadow. Funded with Anduril's internal capital, the company's oven-sized satellite launched on a SpaceX rideshare mission in July with a package of tech demo payloads: an edge-compute processor, a power-management system adaptable to different mission types, and a long-wave infrared space sensor capable of detecting other objects in orbit. Anduril reported on the success of the tech demo mission Tuesday. The company's satellite, named Anduril-216, flies about 590 km (366 mi) above Earth, spending about one-third of each orbit in darkness. Anduril-216's night passes allow its infrared imager to shine.Read full article Comments

articles.title: ESSAY: What's My Name?
articles.description: Abdul El-Sayed faced Islamophobia and taunts over his name on the campaign trail. Ali Abazeed shares his thoughts and reflections on the ownership and proclamation of one's name to the world.
articles.content: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks at an election night event, early Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026, in Detroit. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson / AP)Ali Abazeed is Chief Public Health Officer and Director of the Detroit Health Department for the City of Detroit. He wrote this essay in a personal capacity to share with Michigan Public. You can listen to his reading of the essay above.________________________________________________In February 1967, Muhammad Ali spent fifteen rounds asking his opponent, Ernie Terrell, a question. Terrell had insisted on calling him “Cassius Clay,” a name Ali had set down three years earlier. And so between jabs Ali asked it again and again:“What’s my name?”Ali was the most famous man alive. And still, another man believed he had the authority to decide what he was called. Ali had told Terrell before the fight how it would end.“My name is Muhammad Ali,” he said, “and you will announce it right there in the center of that ring.”When Muhammad Ali died in 2016, I was a fellow at the Detroit Health Department, working for its director, Dr. Abdul El-Sayed. We had both admired Ali, and his death sat heavily on the two of us all week.“Ali’s funeral’s tomorrow. Wanna go?” Abdul asked me after a meeting, as if the plan were already made and only the driving was left.We finished the workday, got in his car, and drove to Louisville, taking turns at the wheel while he took calls from the road. Between calls, he played audiobooks at twice their normal speed, and I pretended to keep up. It was Ramadan, and the shawarmas I ordered for us became the iftar we ate on the highway.The service was the Jenazah, the Muslim funeral prayer, held at Freedom Hall, the arena where Ali had fought his first professional bout. Ali had planned it that way years in advance and wanted it open to anyone who came. No stage, no altar. They carried the casket in and set it on the floor facing Mecca while 14,000 people stood behind it. Abdul and I were at the ropes as the body passed, and what rose from the hall were the chants of his name.Ali. Ali. Ali.Not the name on his birth certificate, but the one he had chosen and spent a lifetime insisting on. Then we took our places in the rows and prayed over him.I think about that day more than almost any other from those years working with Abdul, and I finally understand why. We had driven down to watch a nation say a Muslim’s name the way he had told them to say it. Beside me, praying, stood a man who would spend the next decade demanding the same thing. It was not the first time I had prayed beside him. At the office, he would often say, “It’s prayer time. Wanna pray?” and pause the workday for it, the way you stop for anything owed, and then go back to work.In 2017, a commentator on this station, then Michigan Radio, asked listeners to imagine a candidate named “Andy Smith,” while sharing Abdul’s biography and Abdul’s accomplishments. Then the writer revealed whom he meant. The commentary was called “Great candidate, not so great name.” He admired Abdul, and he wrote with sympathy, which is exactly what stays with me. To help his audience see Abdul’s future, he first had to let them imagine a man who did not have to carry Abdul’s name.The life arrived as a promise, but the name landed as a problem.A year later, when Abdul ran for governor, my friend and I wrote about “The Myth of Viability”: Democrats quietly telling Abdul his name and faith made him unelectable. We answered with his résumé: Rhodes Scholar, physician, the man who rebuilt Detroit’s health department after the bankruptcy. Reading that piece now, I recognize the hope in it, that enough accomplishment might finally settle the matter. Those credentials spoke to what kind of governor he would be, but no credential should have been asked to explain why a Muslim could be one.This year the names came from much higher up. Senator John Kennedy of Louisiana said Abdul slept in “a bin Laden jersey,” and Mike Rogers chuckled beside him. The president called him “Muhammad” over and over, and when someone asked why, he said he felt like it.“I’m the president,” he told a rally. “I can call you whatever the hell I want.”That is the whole argument, stated plainly. The question was never whether a name is long or hard to say. It was about who has the authority to say what you are called: you, or someone with the power to make a room laugh. Terrell believed he had that power. The president believes he has it.Abdul and I never talked about the use and misuse of his name during the campaign. We didn’t have to. I know him well enough to recognize a man persevering, and I knew what it was costing him. I kept thinking of the children who heard the president make a joke of a name like theirs, and of the people who say those children’s names with love.Abdul’s race for U.S. Senate was called at 2:27 in the morning. I was home; I had an early meeting waiting at the Detroit Health Department, which I now run, in the same role Abdul once held. History doesn't excuse you from the morning meeting, but I stayed up late and watched my friend take the stage in victory. A few minutes in, he returned a year’s worth of favors and called the president by his first name.“Donald, look, I know you struggled with my name.”Of all the names available to the president, the one he had reached for to taunt Abdul was Muhammad.Ten years ago, after Muhammad Ali’s funeral, we drove straight to my mother’s house in Dearborn. The sun was setting, and that is where I broke my fast. Abdul met my family that night. I don’t remember exactly what Mama served; it would have been the Syrian food I grew up on, lamb simmered in yogurt and ladled over rice, a salad of torn bread and tomatoes, more of everything than anyone could finish. I remember what she called him.Abdul. Abdulrahman. Habibi.My mother had no use for Andy Smith. In her kitchen, a name was not a problem to be solved. It was what you called a man when you wanted him to come to the table.A name is the only thing a person owns entirely. It was Abdul’s before the scholarship and the medical degree, before the department and the campaign, and it will be his when all of those are lines in someone else’s history. Everything else on a résumé is conferred by people who could have withheld it, but a name is not conferred. It is announced.And that is what a name authorizes: to be called by it. By your mother, by the imam over your body, and by the clerk of the United States Senate when the roll is called in January. Ali knew that in 1967. Louisville heard it in 2016. Michigan felt it on November 3.In the small hours of November 4, in Detroit, Abdul opened the way Muhammad Ali had promised Terrell it would end, in the center of the ring.“My name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed.”Senator-Elect from the State of Michigan._______________________________________________Editor's note: The 2017 opinion piece - “Great Candidate, Not So Great Name” - published by Michigan Public was referenced by Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign for U.S. Senate in 2026 as an example of the latent Islamophobia he would have to overcome to win office. El-Sayed won his bid for the Senate on 11/3/2026, having faced a counter campaign of both blatant and latent Islamophobia. Michigan Public regrets publishing an opinion that contributed to the proliferation of those xenophobic ideas. Michigan Public does not stand by the idea that a person's name should inhibit their ability to run for public office.

articles.title: United Airlines moves to block AI agents from its platform over security concerns
articles.content: United Airlines said on Wednesday it would restrict AI bots' access to its digital platforms, citing data security, in the latest pushback against AI agents increasingly capable of planning and booking trips for travelers. Companies across industries are taking divergent approaches to the rapid rise of AI agents capable of carrying out tasks on behalf of users — some restricting access to protect their platforms, others embracing partnerships. Meanwhile, online travel firms such as Expedia and Booking are working with ChatGPT-parent OpenAI. United warned that sharing account credentials with third-party AI assistants could expose sensitive information and lead to unintended purchases, account modifications or the unauthorized use of frequent-flyer miles. It also said automated AI tools performing actions like flight check-in — which requires human acknowledgment for prohibited items such as explosives — could create regulatory risks. The carrier said it would take steps to restrict access both directly through its digital platforms and indirectly through travel agencies and aggregators, including updates to its booking, ticketing and distribution policies.

articles.title: Energy costs among top issues for battleground voters, polling finds
articles.description: In the wake of Democrats’ sweeping victories across the nation, post-election polling commissioned by organizations focused on clean energy and environmental issues found that energy affordability was at the top of many voters’ minds as they cast their ballots. On Tuesday, Climate Power, a strategic communications organization focused on building support for climate action, shared […]
articles.content: Gas prices at a Speedway gas station in Lansing, Sept. 25, 2026. (Photo by Kyle Davidson/Michigan Advance)In the wake of Democrats’ sweeping victories across the nation, post-election polling commissioned by organizations focused on clean energy and environmental issues found that energy affordability was at the top of many voters’ minds as they cast their ballots. On Tuesday, Climate Power, a strategic communications organization focused on building support for climate action, shared polling data examining how energy costs shaped the midterm results. Climate Power, alongside the League of Conservation Voters, EDF Action and the NRDC Action Fund, commissioned Hart Research for an online survey of 1,778 individuals across 62 competitive U.S. House districts who had either voted, or were certain they would be voting. Breaking down the findings at a press briefing, Jay Campbell, a partner at Hart Research, said while voters were ready to be done with Republicans and President Donald Trump, that rejection did not mean that battleground district voters were enthusiastic about Democrats. Survey results showed 61% of respondents had negative feelings about Donald Trump, while 57% expressed negative feelings toward congressional Republicans. Even though Democrats won majorities in both the U.S. House and Senate, 46% of voters still held a negative perception of Democrats while 41% said they held positive feelings towards the incoming majority party. Graphic from Hart Research showing results from a recent exit poll of voters conducted from Oct. 26 to Nov. 6, 2026. (Screenshot) As for the takeaway from these responses, Campbell said the people are giving Democrats a chance in Congress, and that they would need to take on that mantle and prove themselves. Looking into the issues that were most pressing for voters, the cost of food and groceries “blew everything else out of the water,” Campbell said, with 66% of all voters surveyed listing that as their top issue. However, two separate energy issues were among the top four concerns for voters. Just below the cost of groceries was the cost of gasoline, which was a deciding factor for 41% of voters. The cost of utilities, such as electricity and heating, was the fourth-most prominent issue for voters, with 32% of survey respondents noting it was a key issue in determining their congressional vote. “The long and short of it is the cost of food and groceries, the cost of gasoline, the cost of heating, these are what people need to see Democrats working on going forward,” Campbell said. “The affordability crisis is very real, and energy is very much a part of it.” When asked how the United States produces, delivers and manages energy, 58% of voters said the U.S. should have different policies and approaches from those put forward by Trump, while 28% said that the country should stay the course. Polling from Hart Research examining voter attitudes towards various groups technologies and their impact on energy prices. (Screenshot) Additionally, respondents were asked who they felt benefited more under the Trump administration’s energy policy, consumers like them, or the oil and gas companies and electrical utilities. Twenty-two percent of voters said they had benefited more from the administration’s energy policy while 78% said the companies had benefited more. “Even when you look at self-identified Republicans, it’s 61 to 39 saying corporations versus people like me have been benefiting,” Campbell said. “That’s a pretty clear and damning sense of where people stand.” Moving forward, 62% of respondents said it should be a priority for Congress to bring down electricity prices, while only 7% said it was not what lawmakers should be working on. Campbell also challenged the notion that clean energy is a liberal-coded idea that only appeals to voters on the far left, noting that a majority of swing district respondents said that clean energy was having a positive impact on energy prices. “Those who voted for a Republican candidate say that using more clean energy rather than less would make energy more affordable by a margin of 40% to 29%,” Campbell said. “Not overwhelming, but very much on the positive side rather than on the negative side.” However, there is work left for Democrats to do, Campbell noted, citing polling data that showed only about a third of voters say Democrats are making things better for consumers. And the voters trust them to do that work, Campbell explained, pointing to a comparison between voters surveyed in January, and the most recent survey, conducted between Oct. 26 and Nov. 6. In January 30% of voters surveyed said they trust Republicans more than Democrats to lower monthly energy bills compared to 26% who had more faith in the Dems. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE However, the more recent survey found 43% of respondents trusted Democrats to lower their energy bills, compared to 24% who had more faith in the Republicans. In the polling data from October and November, 45% of respondents also said they had more faith that Democrats would prioritize the interests of the consumer over corporate profits compared to 23% who placed their trust on this issue in Republicans. Voters also trusted Democrats more on issues like regulating AI data centers, lowering the cost of gas and diesel and improving the reliability of the electrical grid. “The narrative around these issues has changed dramatically from what we were hearing in previous elections,” Geoff Garin, the president of Hart Research, told reporters at the top of the press briefing. “The old Republican mantras of ‘drill, baby, drill’ and American energy dominance were and are wholly irrelevant to the current energy debate,” Garin continued. “Instead, the energy debate now is focused on Trump’s ill-conceived war, on data centers, on price gouging by oil companies, and on Trump’s war on clean energy. Every one of these elements led to a damning indictment of Republicans and gave Democrats the high ground in the energy debate.”

articles.title: With $720M round, Britain’s Fractile gets a leg up in the race for AI chips
articles.description: Fractile has now become one of the top-funded players in the race for purpose-built AI chips.
articles.content: Fractile, a British startup developing AI chips, has raised a $720 million Series C backed by Britain’s Sovereign AI Fund with hopes of “ensuring the U.K. has a greater stake in the hardware that will underpin its future economy,” its government stated. Alongside the likes of Axelera, Etched, and OLIX, this makes Fractile one of the top-funded startup players in the race for purpose-built AI chips. Such chips are one of several avenues being explored to reduce the cost of inference — aka using increasingly demanding AI models in production. However, Fractile seeks to go beyond hardware with a full-stack approach that also includes a machine learning compiler to maximize the speed at which LLMs will get executed on its chips. As a result, the company frames itself as a frontier AI company, and its latest round led by Thrive Capital, Founders Fund, Lightspeed Venture Partners, and Redpoint was priced accordingly. According to the British government, the valuation was “over £5 billion” — quite possibly $7 billion, a figure reported both by the Financial Times and a Reuters source. Still, Fractile’s main differentiator will arguably be its hardware design. After a pivot, its approach now revolves on DRAM, the most common type of RAM, but stacked on top of each chip in such a way that it is hoping will bypass the usual trade-off between memory and capacity. This trade-off has become more problematic with the rise of agentic AI, as companies seek to perform longer chains of tasks with large models without compromising on speed. As compute struggles to keep up, hopes are high for AI chips, despite their limited availability to date. In a LinkedIn post, Fractile CEO Walter Goodwin wrote that “there is still a lot of work ahead” for the company, and that the new funding will enable the startup to “ship [its] first chips and systems next year.” When you purchase through links in our articles, we may earn a small commission.
