Michigan GOP reckons with Trump, leadership revolt after election drubbing
articles.description: Michigan Republicans are pointing fingers after an historic drubbing in the midterm elections. Some blame Trump, some blame state party leadership. Where does the party go from here?
articles.content: Michigan Republicans lost big last week as voters gave Democrats control over all leavers of power in Lansing As the dust settles, some are looking for a leadership change, arguing the Michigan GOP chair Jim Runestad needs to go Runestad says that national headwinds were simply insurmountable but that the party missed opportunities on messaging LANSING — Michigan Republicans are pointing fingers after a historic drubbing in the midterm elections, sparking calls to oust party leadership and a debate over how closely to align with President Donald Trump in the final two years of his term. “I thought it was going to be bad,” Dennis Lennox, a GOP consultant, told Bridge Michigan. “I didn’t think it would be this bad … It’s the worst performance for the Republican Party in Michigan since the party was founded in 1854.” Democrats who dominated the midterms are poised to take full control of both state government and Congress, though Trump has promised to use his veto pen aggressively at the federal level. Michigan GOP Chair Jim Runestad defended the local operation, saying the state “actually performed better for the Republicans than the nation.” He suggested that national trends were to blame, though admitted missteps in Michigan on populist issues like data centers and government transparency. “It comes down to it being an off-year, coupled with the price of gas, inflation and the war,” Runestad said, calling it a “missed opportunity” for Republican candidates who should have focused more on affordability and transparency issues. Related: Q&A: Michigan’s next House speaker wants ‘transformational’ change How Abdul El-Sayed, Jocelyn Benson won Michigan: Big turnout, Democratic shifts Democrats take full control of Legislature, Michigan government. What to expect But some are pointing the finger back at Runestad. Chris Long, the grassroots vice chair of the Michigan GOP, blasted Runestad in a series of online videos, calling him a “clown” with “no allies” and saying he hopes the party can “find a new chair with new ideas” who has “a real plan to win in 2028.” Long is teasing a run of his own. Republican operatives have floated other names too, including House Speaker Matt Hall, consultant Scott Greenlee and Oakland County Republican Party Chair Vance Patrick — though none have officially confirmed they will challenge Runestad for the post. Long isn’t alone in his criticism of the state party.Donate Republicans lost “because we had zero inspiration or any leadership with our old and broke MIGOP party Chairman,” former co-chair Meshawn Maddock wrote on social media after the election. She blamed “weak leaders and loser consultants still running 2012 style campaigns,” arguing that the party backed Republicans “in name only” who “never fully backed Trump … got crushed, once again.” Blame game Outside of party leadership concerns, some at both the state and federal level say Republicans lost because of Trump, who had historically low approval ratings heading into the midterm election. “The problem is that we are being drowned by what is happening in Washington and coming out of the White House,” Republican strategist Jason Roe told Bridge, adding that Trump did not give conservatives “a message to run on” let alone “a reason for voters to trust us.” Roe worked as a strategist on US Rep. Tom Barrett’s failed reelection campaign in Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, where progressive Democrat Will Lawrence won with 51% of the vote. It wasn’t a matter of fundraising for Barrett — whose race was one of the most expensive congressional contests ever — or the kinds of candidates the GOP recruited for other posts, Roe argued. Instead, he said the issue lay with the president “talking about everything except the issues that voters were talking about.” “If an activist or some leader within the party looks at these results and think it is anything other than what’s happening in Washington, then they are delusional,” Roe added. In his final pitch to Michigan voters, Trump urged them to imagine he was running in the midterm too, and once Republicans lost, he suggested it was because he wasn’t on the ballot. President Donald Trump and Senate candidate Mike Rogers listen as Rep. John James, R-Mich., speaks at an event at the General Motors Proving Ground Monday, July 27, 2026, in Milford, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya) But Trump isn’t to blame, argued Patrick, the Oakland County GOP chair, who has criticized Runestad’s leadership of the state party. The Michigan GOP failed to properly get the word out on statewide contests like the state Supreme Court, which left county parties to try and fill the void, Patrick told Bridge. Republicans fielded “great candidates” this cycle, he added, arguing Trump had delivered on many promises voters could have gotten behind, including securing the nation’s southern border. Republicans need “to do a better job listening to the voters” and their concerns, as well as meeting younger voters where they’re at, but it was the media who “made sure everybody was always fixated on gas prices,” Patrick argued. “It’s not necessarily Trump’s fault,” said Patrick, who’s led the Oakland County GOP since 2023. “Trump doesn’t dictate the price of gas.” Trump did join Israel in starting the Iran War, however. Iran responded by closing the Strait of Hormuz, choking off a key conduit for Middle East oil. The US subsequently set a record for the most days with gas above $4 a gallon in a calendar year. Messaging misstep? Runestad, the Michigan GOP chair, acknowledged some Republicans failed to meet the moment on certain issues, pointing to fervor surrounding data centers as an area where “the ball was dropped, frankly.” Citing traditional wisdom that the party in power at the federal level usually performs poorly during a midterm election, Runestad said he was “not shocked” as results rolled in showing Republicans lost ground across the state — even in areas where Trump had won in 2024. While there was an anti-Trump factor, the losses are also “punishment for us being weak, limp and flaccid” on issues voters cared about like data centers and public corruption, according to Republican state Rep. Jim DeSana, R-Carleton. DeSana was one of a handful of southeast Michigan Republicans to survive a close election, winning another term by about 1,100 votes. “The hyper-partisan strategy of saying Republicans are good and Democrats are bad is not going to succeed going forward,” DeSana said in a statement, arguing the GOP has to “promote a positive vision for America and speak to the people about their ideas of limited government,” constitutional conservatism and “our staunch defense of liberty.” State Sen. Jim Runestad, R-White Lake, reacts during the Michigan Republican Party Convention, Saturday, Feb. 22, 2025, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya) Bitely, who worked for Republican Attorney General Bill Schuette before joining Duggan’s independent campaign, said the GOP needs to take “fresh ideas” into the 2028 presidential election, along with compelling candidates capable of driving young voter turnout. Nationally, 66% of people ages 18-29 voted for a Democratic candidate for the US House, compared to 31% for Republicans, according to an analysis of exit polls from the Center for Information and Research on Civic Learning and Engagement (CIRCLE) at Tufts University. In Michigan, turnout in college towns appeared to help Democrats flip three GOP seats, ousting Barrett in the mid-Michigan 7th Congressional District and Rep. Bill Huizenga in the southwest Michigan-based 4th, while picking up the 10th Congressional District seat held by failed gubernatorial nominee John James. “The Democrats got super lucky with Abdul El-Sayed,” Bitely said, referencing the state’s next US senator. “I know that he didn’t get as many votes as (gubernatorial winner) Jocelyn Benson, but he brought new people to the party. … Young men who were Trump voters voted for Abdul El-Sayed.” How will the party come back from such a loss? Runestad said he’s “100% convinced the Democrats will overplay their hand” while they are in power and drive voters back to the GOP. “I don’t believe it’s even capable for them not to do that. … I think that the voters will have buyer’s remorse about these people being in office.” Looking for leadership While Trump and other Republicans had a solid 2024 in Michigan, the state party has struggled to maintain steady leadership, which experts say has limited its ability to grow a bench of candidates who could win big races. It’s been an issue since the end of Gov. Rick Snyder’s administration, according to Lennox, who said “the institutional Republican Party has become weaker.” If Michigan Republicans vote out Runestad at their next statewide convention in early 2027, the state party would get its fifth chairperson in seven years. “Any chairman of any political party, or any leader of any political caucus, who fails to either win or fails to maintain (a) majority owes it — at least as an ethical principle — to offer up their resignation,” Lennox said. “Whether their resignation is accepted is a different question.” Delegates attend the Michigan Republican Party Convention, Saturday, Feb. 22, 2025, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya) Runestad isn’t considering resignation. Instead, he told Bridge he is “leaning very strongly towards” running for another term as chair. He had to get “an entire operation set up” after taking over a state party with significant debts and virtually no staff, Runestad argued. Greenlee and Patrick, who both previously ran for state party chair, aren’t ruling out running again. Hall did not respond to requests for comment. A “number of people” have reached out to Greenlee and encouraged him to run, he told Bridge,“but I haven’t made any decision yet.” Patrick said he’s focused on the next county convention, “then we’ll see what’s going on after that.” Runstead, though, said he’s not sweating potential challengers. “The more the merrier,” he told Bridge.

articles.title: Stevens only Michigan representative to miss Hegseth vote. What we know
articles.content: The Republican-controlled House voted 211-204 on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, to block an effort to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, sending eight articles accusing him of unlawful military operations and abuse of power to the House Judiciary Committee. Eleven Democrats were among 18 lawmakers who did not vote. Republican Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky, who introduced the impeachment resolution, was the only Republican to oppose referring the charges to committee. All 203 Democrats who voted joined him, while 210 Republicans and independent Rep. Kevin Kiley of California supported the motion. The 11 Democrats recorded as not voting were Julia Brownley, Lou Correa and Nancy Pelosi of California; Laura Gillen of New York; Steven Horsford of Nevada; Jonathan Jackson of Illinois; Brittany Pettersen of Colorado; Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico; Haley Stevens of Michigan; Marilyn Strickland of Washington; and Frederica Wilson of Florida. Update, November 11, 2026: Several Democrats who did not vote have since explained their absence. Reps. Melanie Stansbury of New Mexico, Laura Gillen of New York, Jonathan Jackson of Illinois, Marilyn Strickland of Washington and Brittany Pettersen of Colorado cited traffic delays near the Capitol. Stansbury and Jackson subsequently registered their opposition to the referral in the Congressional Record. Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi attended a Veterans Day event in San Francisco, while Rep. Lou Correa of California remained in his district for a medical procedure. Rep. Steven Horsford of Nevada missed the vote because of a personal emergency, according to his office. Pelosi's spokesperson said she opposed the referral, and several other lawmakers who missed the vote also indicated they would have voted against it. Public explanations for the nonparticipation of Reps. Julia Brownley of California, Haley Stevens of Michigan and Frederica Wilson of Florida had not been verified as of Wednesday. The vote prevented Massie from forcing separate House votes on the impeachment charges, effectively ending his effort during the current Congress. Hegseth remains defense secretary, with the resolution referred to the Judiciary Committee. Massie introduced eight articles of impeachment Monday, accusing Hegseth of violating federal law and constitutional limits on military authority during operations in Iran, Yemen and Venezuela. The resolution also alleged unlawful killings during strikes against suspected drug-trafficking vessels, failures to protect civilians and retaliation against Democratic Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona over his statements about unlawful military orders. Hegseth rejected the allegations during a Pentagon news conference earlier Tuesday, describing the impeachment effort as a political stunt and defending military operations carried out under President Donald Trump. Following the vote, Trump celebrated the defeat of the impeachment effort and praised Hegseth's leadership. Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell called the referral a victory for the defense secretary and said the department would defend his actions before the Judiciary Committee. House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries had supported impeachment, while Republican leaders backed the referral. Democrats, who won control of both chambers in the November midterm elections, will assume their new congressional majorities in January 2027. Massie first introduced the impeachment effort in September before reviving it through a procedural mechanism that required House action within two legislative days. The Kentucky Republican, who is leaving Congress in January, said Tuesday's referral would effectively end the effort during the current session. The impeachment process requires a simple majority in the House to approve at least one article, followed by a Senate trial where a two-thirds vote is necessary for conviction and removal from office. Tuesday's procedural vote prevented the charges from advancing to that stage. The eight articles remain before the House Judiciary Committee. Democrats could introduce a new impeachment resolution when the next Congress convenes in January, with Jeffries already on record supporting the effort against Hegseth. articles.content: A pickup truck lats down thick exhaust as it passes a rally outside Howell City Hall held in response to recent white supremacist demonstrations on Nov. 23, 2024. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)A Michigan lawmaker has introduced legislation that would make it a crime for drivers to intentionally direct vehicle exhaust at other people, a practice commonly known as “rolling coal.” House Bills 6459 and 6460, introduced Tuesday by state Rep. Brenda Carter (D-Pontiac), would make it illegal to intentionally aim vehicle exhaust at individuals and establish sentencing guidelines for the offense. Rolling coal involves modifying a diesel-powered vehicle to emit thick, dark exhaust smoke. The modifications, often achieved by tampering with a vehicle’s emissions-control equipment, allow a driver to direct the resulting smoke at pedestrians, cyclists or occupants of other vehicles. It has also occurred at political protests, including last year in Howell. Michigan already has a law making it a felony to operate or possess a motor vehicle equipped with a device to produce excessive smoke or gas. This new legislation would address the intentional targeting of individuals with that exhaust, rather than the equipment used to produce the excess emissions. HB 6459 would add a new section to the Michigan Penal Code, making a first offense a misdemeanor with a maximum 93 day jail sentence and/or a $500 fine. A second offense would also be a misdemeanor, but with a maximum one year in jail and/or a $1,500 fine. A third offense, however, would be a felony punishable by up to two years in prison and/or a fine of up to $2,500. HB 6460 would add the proposed offense to the state’s criminal sentencing guidelines. While the bills are tie-barred, meaning one could not take effect without the other, they were both immediately sent to the House Committee of Government Operations, usually a repository for legislation with little to no hope of getting a committee hearing, much less making it to the House floor for a vote.

articles.content: The Trump administration’s fight to stop suspected leaks of top-secret military information on LinkedIn can’t sweep in “a vast number of confidential sources” of random journalists “who have no conceivable relationship” to the Department of Justice’s investigation, an appeals court ruled Tuesday. The order came after the DOJ asked LinkedIn to turn over 18 months of communications from targeted journalists who collectively published more than 1,000 articles on many different topics over that time period. The request was not limited to journalists involved in a controversial report from a news outlet that Trump said exposed confidential military information in a foreign country. (The outlet is not being named to protect national security secrets.) Instead, the DOJ cast a wide net, requesting extensive LinkedIn data on journalists who had any possible link to the journalists around the time the report was drafted. The majority of journalists have LinkedIn accounts and publish their contact information to encourage sources to connect on the platform, LinkedIn argued. So allowing that government overreach went beyond harming targeted journalists and threatened to undermine a critical platform where journalists frequently connect with confidential sources, judges ruled. Even more concerning, the Trump administration secured a secrecy order barring LinkedIn from telling anyone about the sweeping request for a year. That left journalists unaware for far too long that their First Amendment rights had been compromised, judges ruled.Read full article Comments

articles.title: OpenAI’s quarterly revenue reportedly crosses $10B for the first time
articles.description: Sales of $10 billion represents an almost 50% jump from revenue of $6.7 billion the company recorded in the second quarter.
articles.content: OpenAI is bouncing back from the doldrums it experienced earlier this year. The company’s quarterly revenue crossed $10 billion for the first time, thanks to strong demand for its recent AI models, Bloomberg reported, citing anonymous sources. If true, that would represent an almost 50% jump from the $6.7 billion in sales the company reportedly recorded in the second quarter. That would also mark a sizable increase in its revenue growth rate, which was previously said to be about 18% between the first and second quarters of the year. OpenAI’s profitability picture also appears to have improved, with its adjusted operating margin narrowing from -150% in the second quarter to -109% in the third quarter, the report said. OpenAI, one of the first to commercialize AI models, wasn’t exactly struggling to continue growing its top-line expansion — 18% growth on top of $5.7 billion in quarterly revenue is massive by any measure, especially compared to most software businesses. But it was seeing those gains be trumped by its archrival Anthropic, which has taken the lead in capturing the enterprise market for AI models and recently reported Q3 revenue of $17 billion. OpenAI’s broader focus helped it attract a large user base and gain popularity early on, and it says it has over a billion users, but it’s reasonable to assume most of those are free users or subscribers to its cheapest plans. Still, the company lagged Anthropic in catering to enterprises, a market where the Claude maker has pulled ahead, at least in terms of revenue growth. OpenAI has recently benefited from a combination of tighter pricing, discounts, improving models, and a greater focus on building more enterprise-focused products and AI agents that can help people complete tasks. OpenAI has now reached an annual revenue run rate of $50 billion, according to Bloomberg. Meanwhile, Anthropic, which is seeking a $1.4 trillion valuation in an IPO likely to happen soon, said yesterday that its annual revenue run rate had increased by $10 billion within a month to $81 billion as of the end of October. (Note that OpenAI and Anthropic calculate their annualized revenue differently: Anthropic counts sales made by its cloud partners, while OpenAI only reports its share of some sales through its partners.) None of those figures are small, of course, but the companies are also competing with models from Meta, Amazon, Microsoft, and Google, as well as a plethora of cheaper but still highly capable models from open source AI labs, especially those from China. Warren City Council denies rezoning
articles.content: The Warren City Council voted on Tuesday, Nov. 10, to deny a rezoning request meant to open the door for apartments or other multiple-family dwellings to be built on property currently zoned R-1 single family residential. The property on Berg Road south of the Interstate 696 service drive is currently part of the parking lot for the Michigan Institute of Sacred Knowledge. Developer Jamal Khan wants to build three 12-unit buildings and a gazebo on the property. Several residents from the immediate neighborhood surrounding the property in question signed a protest petition, enough to trigger a required super majority of six votes to approve the rezoning. The vote to deny the rezoning request was unanimous. “I have been around for a long time – this is my 11th year on city council – and I don’t think I”ve ever seen a petition with as many signatures to trigger a super-super majority,” City Council Secretary Mindy Moore said. “I appreciate everyone that has come forward and given their viewpoint.” Moore read the council’s motion to deny into the record and detailed the reasons the council denied the rezoning. Incompatibility with the city’s master plan and the impact an R3 multiple family zoning could have on the neighborhood were two of the factors that led the council to its decision. Once a property is rezoned, all uses that fall under that zoning designation – in this case R3 multiple family dwelling district – are allowed. According to Warren’s zoning ordinance, efficiency apartments, multiple family dwellings, boarding, rooming and lodging houses, tourist homes, private garages, and community garages are all allowed under the R3 designation. Moore said the council considered the concerns of the residents about density, traffic, privacy and the effect on property values. “The question is, should we approve R3 zoning which will allow every use in that designation,” Moore said. “This decision rests on land use designation.” The council also considered access to sewers, roads, water and other public services. Moore said there was no confirmation from the city that the current infrastructure would be able to handle the use that an R3 development would bring. “The council finds no changed conditions that would support a rezoning,” Moore said. After Moore finished reading her motion to deny, the audience applauded before being told by Council President Angela Rogensues that applause is disruptive.

El Salvador's Bukele makes a political gamble with a Haiti gang offensive ahead of an election
articles.description: El Salvador's Bukele makes a political gamble with a Haiti gang offensive ahead of an election AP News Haitian PM praises El Salvador after joint strike on alleged home of gang leader BBC Haiti: Haiti and El Salvador Governments Must Ensure Salvadoran Military Personnel Respect Human Rights Amnesty International USA El Salvador is exporting the ‘Bukele model’ to Haiti – but the gang offensive is a gamble for both nat
articles.content: MEXICO CITY (AP) — Salvadoran troops bombard a gangster’s home from helicopters over the Haitian countryside. Civilians cheer on marching camouflage-clad soldiers. Armored cars drive through the Caribbean nation’s gang-ravaged streets. The videos flood the social media of Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele, Salvadoran officials and an army of pro-government influencers with a simple message in a mix of Haitian Creole, English and Spanish: “We will help you take back your country ... Finally, Haiti will be free.” It’s part of Bukele’s push to present himself as the savior to Haiti’s gang crisis. By doing so, experts say the communications specialist-turned-president seeks to defuse mounting international scrutiny over his troops’ deployment and drum up political support in his own country ahead of February elections. But they say the offensive in Haiti is a high-stakes gamble that could both isolate allies like the Trump administration and dent popular support in his own country. “It’s an electoral campaign to promote Nayib Bukele and portray him as if he’s a superhero. They’re selling an Avengers movie,” said Salvadoran political communications strategist Roberto Dubon. “He’s using Haiti as a testing ground to implement his policies on an international level.” El Salvador ’s military offensive in Haiti began in mid-October, when four Salvadoran aviation technicians working with a U.N.-backed mission went missing in a gang attack. Since then, the government has sent 2,500 soldiers to the Caribbean country with little transparency or oversight. The disappearances posed a challenge for Bukele, who gained international fame with a political narrative centered on beating back El Salvador’s gangs with a heavy hand. El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele speaks at the National Palace as he hosts a meeting with U.S. congresspeople in San Salvador, El Salvador, Jan. 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Salvador Melendez, File) El Salvador’s President Nayib Bukele speaks at the National Palace as he hosts a meeting with U.S. congresspeople in San Salvador, El Salvador, Jan. 19, 2026. (AP Photo/Salvador Melendez, File) As international scrutiny has mounted over the operation and a gang leader said that the four technicians are dead, the president’s narrative has shifted from rescuing the Salvadorans to eradicating Haiti’s gangs. “We kept our promise,” Bukele posted on Tuesday, sharing a video of Salvadoran forces bombing a gang leader’s house after previously asking for the coordinates on X. “Most of them ran away without even trying to fight. What cowards!” The tongue-in-cheek tone and images of soldiers mirror cinematic videos the government produces in its own country to craft a careful narrative around Bukele’s gang crackdown, which has fueled accusations of mass human rights abuses. In Haiti, just like in El Salvador, throngs of pro-government influencers quickly latched onto and magnified that message, said Dubon. Meanwhile, Bukele gears up for February presidential elections, which he is all but guaranteed to win with fierce support for his crackdown on gangs. Polling puts approval for the president well over 90%. Democratic concerns hang over the vote after the legislature controlled by Bukele’s party moved up elections from 2029 to 2027 and eliminated presidential term limits in the constitution — paving the way for the populist to stay in power indefinitely. In the face of democratic criticisms, a lagging economy and Salvadorans normalizing newfound freedoms after years of not living in constant fear of the gangs, the Haiti offensive offers Bukele a tool to remind Salvadorans of his security wins ahead of the vote, said Luis Enrique Amaya, a Salvadoran security consultant. “He has to construct this narrative of success (in Haiti) to strengthen his image as president,” Amaya said. “Bukele won’t allow even a centimeter of his popularity and legitimacy to be lost. Not even a millimeter, not a single vote.” Bukele has toyed with the idea of taking his contentious anti-crime campaign abroad for years, but his current offensive is increasingly seen as a risky bet. A soldiers from El Salvador looks out from a convoy of armored vehicles carrying military personnel in the Tabarre neighborhood of Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Odelyn Joseph) A soldiers from El Salvador looks out from a convoy of armored vehicles carrying military personnel in the Tabarre neighborhood of Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Friday, Oct. 30, 2026. (AP Photo/Odelyn Joseph) On Monday, the rights group Amnesty International called on El Salvador and Haiti’s governments to publicly disclose the agreement allowing forces into Haiti, and to “comply with international human rights law.” It warned of operations potentially exacerbating violence and affecting civilians. The same day, Bukele ally U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio distanced himself from the Salvadoran offensive when speaking to the press, saying the U.S. was “not actively involved.” He threw his support behind the U.N.-backed gang suppression force, of which El Salvador doesn’t form part. Others, including Haiti’s prime minister and the president of the Dominican Republic — which shares an island with Haiti and is providing El Salvador with logistical and intelligence support — threw their support behind Bukele. Dominican President Luis Abinader on Tuesday called on the U.N.-backed force to coordinate its actions with El Salvador’s troops to “decisively support the Salvadoran military and the attitude of President Bukele.” Security experts like Diego Da Rin, Haiti analyst for International Crisis Group, have cast doubt on Bukele’s ability to replicate his model to vanquish Haiti’s gangs. Bukele debilitated El Salvador’s two powerful gangs by suspending key constitutional rights and detaining more than 1% of the small Central American nation’s population. The Salvadoran investigative news organization El Faro, whose staff has since been exiled from the country, also reported that Bukele had negotiated with those gangs. Haiti’s gang warfare is far more convoluted. Roughly two dozen well-known gangs operate in Port-au-Prince and dozens more have launched deadly attacks outside the capital. They have spent years leeching off political turmoil and overwhelmed police forces to make power grabs and sow terror. They wield weapons smuggled mainly from the U.S. and are far more well-armed than Salvadoran gangs once were. They are deeply entwined with some of the country’s political elite, making it nearly impossible for Bukele to replicate his war on gangs. A moto-taxi driver runs past armored vehicles in the Tabarre neighborhood of Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Odelyn Joseph) A moto-taxi driver runs past armored vehicles in the Tabarre neighborhood of Port-au-Prince, Haiti, Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. (AP Photo/Odelyn Joseph) That will either push Salvadoran troops into an extended conflict or, more likely, push Bukele to make quick shows of force to project victory before retiring troops, said Tiziano Breda, an analyst with Armed Conflict Location & Event Data. Breda warned that costs incurred by the foreign offensive — Bukele’s government has said it’s footing the bill — could fester resentment in El Salvador, where one in four people still live in poverty. Da Rin said that Salvadoran troops could pressure Haitian police and international forces to better organize and more effectively push back the gangs, something they have failed to do for years. But he warned it could also push rival gangs to unite and form coalitions, as has happened in the past. Similar to El Salvador’s own war on gangs, that could have a human toll, he warned, especially if Salvadoran troops don’t operate under strict rules like the U.N.-backed force. “The Salvadoran troops’ eagerness to secure quick, symbolic victories entails huge risks for civilians who can be caught in the crossfire,” Da Rin said. articles.content: Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself. Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app, Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code. More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. articles.description: Scott Parrott, University of South Carolina When the voice came over the plane’s PA system, it seemed familiar yet surprising: “Hello, everybody.” “What?!” a passenger shouted, shocked. Others laughed and rose from their seats as former President Barack Obama appeared in person and welcomed the airplane of veterans to Washington before Veterans Day in 2025. […]
articles.content: Uniformed participants march during the Veterans Day parade in Manhattan on Nov. 11, 2025. Stephani Spindel/VIEWpress/Corbis News via Getty Scott Parrott, University of South Carolina When the voice came over the plane’s PA system, it seemed familiar yet surprising: “Hello, everybody.” “What?!” a passenger shouted, shocked. Others laughed and rose from their seats as former President Barack Obama appeared in person and welcomed the airplane of veterans to Washington before Veterans Day in 2025. They had flown from Wisconsin to Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport aboard an Honor Flight to see the capital’s monuments to military service. “I wanted to stop by and just say thank you for your extraordinary service – to you, your family,” Obama said in brief remarks later posted to social media. “The sacrifices that all of you made to protect our country is something that will always be honored.” Obama’s post was one of 399,000 references to veterans on the social media platform X on Veterans Day last year, Nov. 11, 2025. The annual holiday was established to “solemnly remember the sacrifices of all those who fought so valiantly on the seas, in the air and on foreign shores, to preserve our heritage of freedom,” as President Dwight D. Eisenhower proclaimed. The hundreds of thousands of posts are compelling to me as a social scientist who studies how veterans are represented in the media. The volume of commentary illustrates Americans’ desire to recognize veterans, but it also captures the transience of public attention. By the following Tuesday, Nov. 18, 2025, the number of references to veterans plummeted by 374,000, or nearly 94%. The news cycle had moved on. The shift was not particularly surprising. My research shows that social media mentions of veterans peak in positive sentiment at two points each year: Veterans Day and Memorial Day. The rest of the time, the conversations on social media are largely driven by news outlets releasing stories and politicians announcing programs and events. Indeed, social and other mass media play a role in what experts describe as a military-civilian gap. Put simply, while U.S. adults hold the military in high regard, they do not understand the institution or the experiences of its personnel despite its importance in domestic and international affairs and its US$900 billion in taxpayer funding. This military-civilian gap can create problems when it comes to military recruitment, civilians’ ability to identify with neighbors who serve and veterans reintegrating into civilian society. The military-civilian gap The military-civilian gap exists in part because, since the draft ended in 1973, the share of Americans who have served in the armed forces has declined. Only about 6% of adults were veterans in 2022, a decline from 18% in 1980. Compounding the issue, a decreasing proportion of U.S. adults personally know someone who has served. That means much of the population is learning about military life through mass media representation. Journalists gravitate toward stories in which the subject matter is timely, emotional or full of conflict, because these qualities engage audiences. They operate on tight deadlines with limited resources. They also face restricted access to the Pentagon. That means news outlets may be more inclined to cover a holiday, charity event or violent crime involving veterans than to take deep dives into the military budget or examine the role of veteran-owned businesses in the local economy. Because of this, veterans end up typecast as heroes or victims of their service. Politicians also influence which issues people in the U.S. see in the news or discuss on social media, but the share of members of Congress with military experience has plummeted since the 1970s. Posts about veterans surge around Nov. 11, then drop off within a week. AP Photo/Matt Slocum Veterans in the media In a 2018 study, our research team examined how news organizations in all 50 states represented veterans in news stories shared on X. In analyzing 1,460 stories, we identified three themes, which together described a majority of stories: veterans as heroes, as recipients of charity, or as victims of mental or physical harm. Some military veterans may be heroes, and some may face challenges related to trauma, reintegrating into civilian society or navigating government bureaucracy. Such coverage may certainly be newsworthy. The problem, according to critics of veterans’ representation in news media, is that not much else appears in the media. As one veteran told a researcher, “It doesn’t sell newspapers that Joe Smith from Davenport went to Afghanistan three times, got out of the military, went to college, and now works as an account manager for American Eagle.” But media representations of social groups shape our perceptions of the world. A 2021 experiment found that exposure to stereotypical news stories about veterans led readers to associate veterans with post-traumatic stress disorder, a misunderstood and stigmatized condition. This, in turn, led readers to feel less desire to be socially close with veterans. The outcome illustrated how stories can have unintended downstream consequences even when journalists are covering newsworthy topics – in this case, PTSD and homelessness. We also tested whether reading a second story – one in which veterans talked about media stereotypes – would dampen those negative effects. It worked, illustrating the importance of a news feed that provides nuance. In another study, we asked 1,047 U.S. adults to picture a veteran, describe the veteran and then explain where the image originated. When people depended on media for their image, rather than personal experience, they called to mind stereotypical images such as homelessness, PTSD and heroism. Given these stereotypes, a number of veterans organizations are advocating for broader, more insightful media representation. Military Veterans in Journalism and Veterans in Media & Entertainment are nonprofits that help veterans pursue professional careers in news and entertainment media, motivated in part by the potential for veterans to produce nuanced stories about military life. There are also nonprofit news organizations, such as The War Horse, seeking to bridge the military-civilian gap through storytelling and investigative reporting. Beyond ‘thank you’ Media can draw attention to veterans. Obama’s airport surprise racked up 10.8 million views, 136,000 likes and 18,000 shares on X. But it will take more than made-for-media moments to bridge the military-civilian gap. That includes taking conversations with veterans offline. In a 2019 study, U.S. Air Force Maj. Nicholas J. Mercurio conducted focus groups with veterans and active-duty service members and asked how they felt about “reflexive and formulaic expressions of gratitude” from the public such as “thank you for your service.” Responses were mixed, in part because veterans assumed civilians did not understand what that service entailed. Nonetheless, there was general agreement that civilians could go beyond thank you by showing interest in the personal experiences of veterans and having sincere conversations about their jobs. In doing so, civilians can demonstrate “interest in the individual,” Mercurio wrote, “not what they represent.” Scott Parrott, Professor of Media Effects, School of Journalism and Mass Communications, University of South Carolina. Now, multiple items related to the project are slated for Thursday’s Planning and Economic Development committee. These include, but are not limited to: The community benefits report for the Renaissance Center/East Riverfront Project. The actual Community Benefits Provisions. Public hearing on the issue. A tax abatement request to establish a commercial rehabilitation district for the project. Memos from council members seeking information about the project, the feasibility of community requests (including, namely, revenue sharing), the community benefits ordinance, and other items. A privileged and confidential memo from the city’s Law Department on revenue sharing and community ownership for certain developments that trigger a community benefits process. WORD ON THE STREET? Residents online and in meetings have been largely railing against the development for weeks. Concerns have been raised about the lack of community demands being met, over-privatization of the downtown and riverfront space, how the planned decade of construction will impact Detroiters and more. The most public support for the project has come from some city seniors and youth who seem hungry for revitalization and entertainment downtown. Mayor Mary Sheffield and her administration have expressed public support for the redevelopment and developers in social media posts. She has also been quoted as highlighting the importance of “the people’s waterfront,” and that Detroiters should see “some” of what they want there. During Tuesday’s session, the main issue uniting commenters’ concerns was time. Longtime sailor District 5 Amy Hubbarth said she is deeply passionate about the potential of developing marina, but does not feel like she has seen solid plans from developers so far. “I want development,” she stressed to me, echoing comments she made during the meeting. “They (council members) need to take their time.” The $2.2 billion project, proposed by Bedrock and General Motors, calls for two of the five Renaissance Center towers to come down. Bedrock and GM are seeking tax breaks and development incentives worth $548 million and have said the project can’t be done without them. Last month, businessman Dan Gilbert pledged $1 billion to create a new nonprofit to redevelop and run the Renaissance Center and east riverfront. Another commenter, Tahira Ahmad, called in to voice her disappointment about the development, asking council members not to let “Dan Gilbert steal our two towers” and to take their time considering the issue. District 4 resident Eden Bloom, an environmental advocate who works with the Detroit People’s Platform, has frequently weighed in on the RenCen development at meetings and online. Like many other commenters Tuesday, Bloom was cut off mid-comment. He was able to list his criticisms, including the amount of the actual direct benefits compared to the $548 million of public support being sought for the project. He also joined many residents calling for the confidential memo to be made public. HOW CAN I LEARN MORE OR MAKE MY VOICE HEARD? The committee meeting where these items will be discussed is Thursday Nov. 12, at 10 a.m. You can attend and/or comment in-person on the 13th floor of the Coleman A. Young Municipal Center, or virtually here: https://detroitmi.gov/government/city-clerk/city-council-agendas-documents. STUDY UP. articles.title: Detroit selects five new honorary street signs. Here’s who made the list
articles.description: A voice, a bluesman, an education giant, an Emmy-winner and a good neighbor: Meet your 2026 Secondary Street Sign awardees.
articles.content: Detroit’s City Council chose five legendary Detroiters whose names will adorn street signs throughout the city. After a public hearing, lengthy public comment during Tuesday’s formal session and three rounds of voting, the following legacies are set to be honored from a list of 20 new and returning nominees: Returning nominees: Martha Jean “The Queen” Steinberg, Andrew L. Starks Sr. and Ernest Harden Jr. Steinberg was among the nominees who received the most support from attendees at both the public hearing and council session. Around twenty of the nearly 70 in-person and call-in commenters on Tuesday leant their voices for her during the 30 seconds they were limited to do so. Many in person supporters came armed with decorated handfans they waved silently whenever she was mentioned. Supporters spoke about the Black radio pioneer’s generational impact and commitment to the city through outreach, mentoring, and more. This included her 48-hour radio broadcast during the 1967 rebellion, something more than one community member has credited with saving the city — and themselves. “If it wasn’t for the Queen, I swear to God, I don’t know where I’d be, because her leadership and the way she taught me how to learn to love God for myself is the only reason why I’m standing here today at 56 years old,” said speaker Rico Jackson. Tyrone Jackson, who noted Steinberg’s history of working with city officials to improve Detroit, said he couldn’t think of, “a more fitting and more honorable way” to thank Steinberg for “all that she’s done for all of us.” Steinberg’s sign will be at the intersection of Monica Street and Grand River Avenue in District 7. A military veteran and one of the first Black pilots licensed at Detroit City Airport, Rose Jones had been neighbors with Starks since April 1989. She said she has watched the centenarian seek to improve and sustain his community for decades. Starks helped foster generational wealth and homeownership in his community amid the “white flight” of the 1970s. He did this by buying vacant properties, and selling them below-market to new homeowners. “We often look for heroes in the midst of us. Mr. Starks is a gentle giant and quiet mover, a sterling example of everyday heroes,” Jones said during the Oct. 23 public hearing. “… Mr. Starks never sought accolades or attention, but was pleased to be a testament for us of hope, resilience and fortitude, which we all wish that all Detroit residents would strive to imitate.” Starks’ sign will be at the intersection of St. Patrick and Gunston avenues in District 4. Starks and fellow awardee Ernest Harden Jr. are the only recipients this year who have lived to see their names chosen. It took two rounds of run-off voting to secure Harden Jr. his spot. The 73-year-old actor, who has been lauded for his Emmy Award-winning role in the medical drama “The Pitt,” has been appearing in classic TV shows and movies for decades. This includes The Jeffersons, Taxi Driver, White Men Can’t Jump, among others. According to official committee documents, Harden Jr. also supported arts programming and took part in mentorship here in Detroit as well. Harden Jr.’s sign will be at the intersection of St. Aubin and Cody streets in District 3. First-time applicants: Tyrone Winfrey Sr. and Luther “Bad Man” Keith Education advocate Tyrone Winfrey Sr. and award-winning Detroit News reporter Luther “Badman” Keith will also get signs. Winfrey and Keith were nominated for the first time this year. Detroit resident and former Detroit police commissioner William Davis offered his support for Keith Tuesday alongside another nominee, calling him an outstanding Detroiter and saying that his effect on the community will live on. Keith’s work, he said, was “outstanding” and continued until the day that he died. Edwina King, an associate director in legislative affairs and equitable development for the city, called in a personal capacity to lend her support to Winfrey. King said the work Winfrey performed for youth and families in education and public service — including through the Detroit Public School Community District, the University of Michigan and Greater Grace Temple, where he served as deacon — reflects a life dedicated to making a difference. “A secondary street sign (for Winfrey) is more than just a sign,” she said. “it’s a symbol of gratitude, a testament of service.” Those signs will be located at the intersection of Pickford and Indiana avenues in District 3 and Livernois Avenue and Eight Mile, respectively. The sign selections come as some council members raise the prospect of amending the selection process going forward. Council Member Latisha Johnson recently proposed a pause in secondary street signs for 2027 to consider changes, including options to reduce the bottleneck of applicants for just a handful of annual signs. Also honored at the meeting was the legacy of Dr. Janese Champman, the former leader of the Detroit Historic Advisory Board and a “shepherd of the process.” The former Secondary Street Sign manager died suddenly earlier this year, and was honored by Council President James Tate during the meeting for her “thumbprint” on the process. “We just want to again lift her name up, her memory. And who knows? Maybe in a couple years we will have her being considered (for a secondary street sign) as well,” Tate said. Many attendees of Tuesday’s meeting echoed concerns raised by Johnson, expressing discontent with the selection process, including the shortened public comment time and the volume of nominees. Also voicing issues was Council President Pro Tempore Coleman A. Young II, who said he took issue with certain parts of the rigid ordinance, like the five-year limit for nominees to be carried over if they are not selected. Johnson, chair of the subcommittee that handles the public hearings for secondary street sign nominations, assured Young and residents that a push for changes was already in the works. Council is currently considering a pause on accepting new applications for 2027 to allow time to consider the current rollover applicants, as well as possible amendments to the process. “We are, as a matter of fact, looking to amend the process, hopefully, to make it a little easier on us and a little easier on you (residents) as we continue to move forward, because there are so many people who deserve a secondary street sign throughout the city of Detroit,” Johnson said.

States are counting on battery farms. Some towns don’t want them.
articles.description: SNOQUALMIE, Wash. — In the race to meet the nation’s growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new “battery farms” that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition. The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they […]
articles.content: A battery storage facility sits in front of wind turbines near Palm Springs, California. States and utilities are building battery farms but many communities oppose them. (Photo by Mario Tama/Getty Images)SNOQUALMIE, Wash. — In the race to meet the nation’s growing power demands, states and utilities are rapidly building new “battery farms” that can store energy for when customers need it most. But as the facilities grow, so too does community opposition. The systems store banks of batteries in buildings or shipping containers. While they can take many forms, developers are increasingly building large, multi-acre projects designed to meet the needs of local utilities. The electricity stored by such systems nationwide has grown tenfold since 2022, and it’s projected to double again by the end of 2028. State lawmakers and renewable energy advocates say battery storage is urgently needed to stabilize the grid and support the transition to clean power. But in some communities, residents are wary of proposals to build industrial battery systems in their neighborhoods, noting that battery fires can produce toxic smoke and are difficult to extinguish. As the backlash has grown, nearly 200 communities have passed or proposed moratoriums to block battery farms from being built near them. Backers say modern systems are designed to be much safer than previous versions, with data showing that fire risk has dropped significantly. But some industry leaders fear the perception of danger — along with a rising tide of community activism stirred by the buildout of data centers — could threaten an industry that’s becoming integral to the nation’s energy future. ‘Meteoric growth’ Most energy storage on the U.S. grid takes the form of battery energy storage systems, commonly known as BESS. Such facilities host banks of batteries, typically lithium-ion — a technology that has become more capable and cost-effective with the development of electric vehicles. At present, battery storage capacity nationwide exceeds 50 gigawatts, up from just 5 gigawatts at the beginning of 2022. Another 54 gigawatts is slated to come online in the next two and a half years. That projected total of more than 100 gigawatts would be enough to power roughly 75 million homes, although battery farms are designed to provide electricity for one to four hours, as opposed to the more continuous supply of conventional power plants. “The meteoric growth is continuing,” said Noah Roberts, executive director of the U.S. Energy Storage Coalition, an industry group. “For state policymakers who are focused on the energy transition and decarbonizing the grid, (battery) storage is essential.” Policymakers and energy planners have increasingly pushed for battery farms as more renewable energy sources have come online. Solar farms, for instance, can produce massive amounts of cheap electricity during the afternoon hours — but peak demand is in the evening, when people get home from work and turn on household appliances. With batteries on the grid, that surplus solar energy can be stored and saved for when it’s needed, instead of firing up more costly “peaker” gas plants to meet evening demand. Industry leaders say battery systems can also improve reliability and affordability, even in states without clean energy goals. They note that Texas and California are home to a majority of the battery projects on the grid so far. While typically on opposite ends of the political spectrum, both states produce large amounts of wind and solar energy, while facing heavy power demands that have at times required energy conservation measures and put the grid at risk of blackouts. Battery systems, backers say, have already stabilized their grids considerably. Adding to the appeal of battery farms is the fact that they can be put in place quickly, in a matter of months, compared with much longer timelines for other energy projects. “As we’re dealing with a power supply crisis, energy storage is the obvious solution for adding capacity and getting more out of the grid that we’ve already paid for,” Roberts said. State policies have been a driver of the industry’s growth. Thirteen states have enacted targets requiring their utilities to deploy certain amounts of energy storage by specific dates. In Maryland, Democratic Del. Lorig Charkoudian authored a law in 2025 directing state regulators to issue bids for projects totaling 1,600 megawatts of energy storage. “It’s basically a no-regret path,” Charkoudian said in an interview earlier this year. “Over time once we bring more renewables on, they will be that much more valuable because there’s battery storage.” Charkoudian noted that the Trump administration has stalled permitting for offshore wind and other renewable projects, while phasing out clean energy tax credits. The federal push against those forms of energy has made battery farms a more attractive option, as they’ve met with less resistance and still qualify for a 30% tax credit. Community concerns For all of the potential that battery farms offer the grid, some communities are not eager to host them. Much of the opposition centers around the risk for out-of-control fires and toxic smoke. Most prominently, the Moss Landing Power Plant in Monterey County, California, caught fire in early 2025, burned for several days and released 55,000 pounds of toxic metals into nearby wetlands. Lithium-ion batteries, when ignited, can trigger a reaction known as thermal runaway that is nearly impossible to extinguish. Across the country, community activists have been alarmed to see battery farms proposed near schools, playgrounds and senior care facilities. “They’re making us collateral damage,” said Phoenix Artemisia, an activist in Watsonville, California, who has helped lead efforts to oppose a proposed battery storage facility there. “We have 12 schools within two miles of us here, but these out-of-state developers are telling us what we’re going to do in our backyard.” The Watsonville project has stirred up significant community opposition, Artemisia said, prompting the developer to seek approval from state regulators in order to bypass local officials. Industry leaders say the Moss Landing facility was built using an older design, prior to the issuance of safety standards from the National Fire Protection Association that cover most systems on the grid today. Newer projects use an updated battery chemistry that burns at lower temperatures, and store the batteries in isolated, modular containers so that fires don’t spread to nearby units. As a result, battery fires have become much more rare and far less devastating. Earlier this month, the Electric Power Research Institute, an independent nonprofit, published an analysis of battery system failures dating back to 2011. The report found that failures (defined as large thermal events such as arc flashes, fires or explosions) have declined 97% in the U.S. since 2018, when adjusted for the amount of battery power on the grid. The incidents that have happened in new systems have largely remained small and contained, said Lakshmi Srinivasan, who authored the analysis. “Specific design choices have really reduced not only the likelihood of a failure, but the impact of a failure if it happens,” she told Stateline. Srinivasan said the risk profile of battery farms is similar to that of electrical transformers, components of the electrical grid that already exist in many communities. But some communities feel a slim chance of disaster is still too high. Residents in Snoqualmie, Washington, have voiced opposition to a proposed battery project just outside city limits, prompting the city and several neighboring communities to enact moratoriums on such facilities. “We need to think more carefully about what the worst-case scenario is, not just what’s typical,” said Dan Murphy, a council member in the city of Snoqualmie. “The science says (battery farms) are getting safer, but we’re still early.” Amid the local backlash, the developer, Jupiter Power, has indicated that it will pursue approval from state-level energy siting regulators, removing the project from King County jurisdiction. Murphy said his community supports clean energy, but objected to the site location near homes, a playground, a waterway and a critical evacuation route. He said Jupiter Power kept locals in the dark until they thought the project was a done deal. A sign in Snoqualmie, Washington, opposes a proposed battery energy storage system, known as BESS. (Photo by Alex Brown/Stateline) “We are a very reserved and polite community,” he said. “To see the outcry and the animation and the mobilization, it’s really struck a nerve with our residents.” In a document responding to community concerns, Jupiter Power noted that battery farms must be built near substations, which are located in close proximity to the communities they serve. That reality, the company said, makes it unrealistic for local officials to demand that battery systems keep their distance from populated areas. In King County, the company found, all 157 substations that are suitable for a battery project are located within a quarter-mile of schools, daycares, hospitals, natural areas or other sensitive sites. Jupiter Power did not grant an interview request, but referred questions to Clean and Prosperous, a Washington-based nonprofit focused on reducing emissions. “For any battery storage project there will inherently already be energy infrastructure nearby,” said Kelsey Nyland, communications director with Clean and Prosperous. “It often feels like we expect clean energy projects to be perfect in a way that we don’t expect from fossil fuel projects.” Nyland noted that Washington state ranks dead last in the nation for clean energy growth, despite its ambitious climate goals. Battery storage, she said, can help population centers in western Washington harness surplus wind and solar power from rural eastern Washington. She added that Washington has only one operational battery storage facility, making it difficult to alleviate local’s concerns by touring a nearby site. Similar disputes have played out in dozens of communities across the country, and many have passed temporary measures banning the construction of battery storage facilities. Earlier this month, a pair of former economic officials from the Biden administration wrote in The Washington Post that battery farms had been caught in a case of “mistaken identity” amid the nationwide backlash to data centers, which have stirred up similar feelings about industrial siting and environmental risks. But while data centers increase pressure on the grid, battery farms reduce it, they wrote, making the “conflation” an expensive mistake. Some local activists have asked for battery farms to be sited in remote areas, where they would pose fewer risks. But industry leaders say they’re simply following the incentives set forth by utilities, which prioritize projects that can connect to the grid near population centers. “If you have a source of power right where the power’s being consumed, the more efficient your system’s going to be,” Malaquias Encarnacion, managing director with Carina Energy, a development services firm that works on battery storage projects. Carina Energy has tracked 175 battery farm moratoriums enacted or proposed by communities across the country. In some cases, Encarnacion said, those actions have been temporary measures enacted by local governments to give themselves time to learn about the issue. “If I didn’t know anything about it, I would be nervous as well,” he said, encouraging developers to engage with communities early to alleviate those concerns. Stateline reporter Alex Brown can be reached at abrown@stateline.org. articles.title: Mamdani Budget Floats on Wall Street Cash as Momentum Grows for New Taxes
articles.content: Find our headlines more quickly in Google search results. When the City Council and Mayor Zohran Mamdani agreed on a $127 billion budget last June, the story behind the story was obvious. The numbers for the fiscal year beginning last July 1 added up to a balanced budget, thanks to a flood of state aid and some fiscal gimmicks. And the plan projected a worrisome $6 billion hole for the next budget. But when the mayor updates his budget later this week, he will be the beneficiary of two major developments that will ease his budget problems and, at the same time, get him closer to his long-cherished goal of a tax increase on the wealthy. First, the city has received a flood of tax revenue from Wall Street that will shrink the deficit. And last Friday, newly re-elected Gov. Kathy Hochul opened the door to a tax increase, making it likely the question to be decided in the next state legislative session will not be whether to raise taxes but by how much, on whom and for what reason. Sign up for free morning headlines in your inbox. “I will work hard to manage within our existing resources, but if we need more, we will find a path, as I’ve done before when there’s a particular need, a very specific need,” Hochul said at the annual post-election political gathering in Puerto Rico, linking any increase to the mayor’s plan for universal childcare, which carries a price tag of as much as $9 billion a year. The mayor’s announcement this week, called the November budget modification, is primarily a way to see whether the city is on track to produce a balanced budget. The fiscal watchdog Citizens Budget Commission says a key issue will be whether the Mamdani administration will detail the $1 billion in savings it has instructed city agencies to find. Another key issue will be whether the administration will be able to cut spending in the city’s housing voucher program and at homeless shelters, along with the cost of sending special education students to private schools, as it has pledged. Mayors do not usually change their revenue forecasts, but there is little doubt the city is going to see an increase over what it expected to collect in the current year. The state said last month that soaring Wall Street profits had boosted revenue for its current fiscal year, which ends March 31, by a whopping $8 billion more than projected. Hochul also said the expected deficit for the next budget had plunged to $3 billion from a little over $6 billion.The governor put the windfall into reserves and paying down debt, though the Legislature could always decide to spend that money in the next budget and send some of that money to the city. The city will not see as big a jump since income and corporate taxes comprise a smaller portion of local taxes than the state, but the numbers will go up. City Comptroller Mark Levine reported personal income taxes in the first three months of the city’s fiscal year were $500 million more than expected. Since the revenue surge is almost completely dependent on Wall Street and because the profits it is generating are largely a result of the artificial intelligence boom, fiscal experts warn the windfall could disappear quickly. “The rocky markets of the last few days serve as a reminder that the city needs to prepare itself to protect New Yorkers from the next bust,” said Andrew Rein, president of the Citizens Budget Commission.He said he wants the city to follow the governor’s example and send extra money to its reserve funds in case tax revenue plunges. With Hochul easing her opposition to tax increases, momentum for a hike seems irreversible. Both Assembly Speaker Carl Heastie and Senate Majority Leader Andrea Stewart-Cousins have said they favor an increase on wealthy New Yorkers. New York City residents making more than $2 million currently pay a 14% tax on income, the highest in the nation. articles.description: As tech companies and President Donald Trump’s administration continue pushing to build out more data centers to drive artificial intelligence development, some proposals are looking to move these facilities underwater. Scientific American reported Oct. 27 that the Trump Administration is considering proposals for underwater data centers in Cook Inlet, Alaska, and the Gulf of Maine. […]
articles.content: Big Sable Point Lighthouse (left) and Ludington North Breakwater Light (right) in Ludington, Michigan on July 4, 2026. (Photo by Jon King/Michigan Advance)As tech companies and President Donald Trump’s administration continue pushing to build out more data centers to drive artificial intelligence development, some proposals are looking to move these facilities underwater. Scientific American reported Oct. 27 that the Trump Administration is considering proposals for underwater data centers in Cook Inlet, Alaska, and the Gulf of Maine. While the preliminary permits requested by DeepGreen Holdings LLC would not give the company permission to begin construction, tribal nations and environmental groups have come out in opposition to the proposals, raising concerns about the impacts they could have on ocean temperatures and marine life, including two separate species of endangered whales that live and hunt at the project sites. There are very few underwater data centers in operation across the globe. While Microsoft previously deployed an underwater data center near Scotland’s Orkney Islands to study the feasibility of underwater data centers, the company shuttered the project, with Noelle Walsh, the president of Microsoft cloud operations and innovation, telling Data Center Dynamics in 2024, “I’m not building subsea data centers anywhere in the world.” There are also two underwater data centers operating along the coast of China. While mainland data centers have drawn concerns over their heavy electricity and water usage needed to cool to servers they contain, offshore data centers can use the water they’re immersed in to help cool the equipment. Although the Great Lakes have yet to draw any proposals for underwater data centers, the region has proven attractive for the facilities due to its plentiful freshwater resources. In response, environmental groups and policy experts have put together several recommendations and frameworks for addressing the influx of data center proposals, with the Alliance for the Great Lakes, a nonprofit focused on protecting the region’s waters, stressing that Great Lakes states are in need of a plan when it comes to managing increasing water use. However, if a company were to propose a data center within the Great Lakes, there are guardrails in place, Helena Volzer, the alliance’s director of water resources, told Michigan Advance. While each state does things differently there generally needs to be some kind of permit approval for anything placed on the bottomlands of the Great Lakes, Volzer explained. In addition to state-level permits, there would also need to be permits from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers and the federal government, Volzer explained. While speaking with the Advance, Miyoko Sakashita, the oceans program director at the Center for Biological Diversity, noted that any federal permits also need to comply with the Endangered Species Act, the National Environmental Policy Act and the Clean Water Act. Volzer also pointed to public opposition to data centers within the region as another barrier a hypothetical Great Lakes data center would need to overcome. EGLE takes comments on wastewater permit for onsite water treatment at Saline Township data center “I think if there’s resistance to building them on land for all of the resource reasons, I can only imagine the resistance there might be to building within the lakes themselves,” Volzer said. As far as the environmental impacts, Volzer pointed to the warming of nearby waters as one key concern. “Even in an ocean, you still have that concern. But in a sensitive freshwater ecosystem like the lakes, I would think that would be of even more concern,” Volzer said, noting how warming waters have exacerbated issues with harmful algal blooms in Lake Erie. Temperature changes can also harm fish populations, Volzer noted, explaining that when fish get accustomed to warmer waters, drops in temperature can kill them. Sakashita pointed to habitat impacts and noise pollution as major concerns in the center’s opposition to the proposed data centers in Maine and Alaska. “Many animals are very sensitive to noise for their communication or migration or hunting for food and things like that,” Sakashita said. Construction of an underwater data center would also carry its own risks for pollution and disrupting the ecosystem, Sakashita explained. GET THE MORNING HEADLINES. SUBSCRIBE Both Volzer and Sakashita noted that depending on the design of the data center, these developments could contain harmful chemicals that could pollute the waters. Additionally, the energy source used by the data center could contribute to other environmental impacts, Sakashita explained, noting that the large amounts of power demanded by data centers could result in massive amounts of greenhouse gas pollution if they are powered by fossil fuels. The data centers in Maine and Alaska would be powered by tidal turbines if constructed. Sakashita noted that turbines can trap animal species and kill small organisms like zooplankton, which could hurt the amount of prey available for other species. While Volzer was skeptical of the possibility and the feasibility of a data center making its way into the Great Lakes due to the costs, the public perceptions, and the regulations in place, Sakashita warned that those guardrails are under threat. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act, proposed in the U.S. Senate, contains rollbacks to the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act, Sakashita explained, noting that tribal nations and states like Michigan could lose their authority over projects like an underwater data center if the bill becomes law. “It’s really important for us to safeguard our bedrock environmental laws because they do give us some tools to make sure that projects like this are not doing a lot of damage to endangered species or to our habitats that are really important for wildlife,” Sakashita said.

articles.description: Good Truckin’ Diner’s departure from its original location in REO Town must have stung for those who live nearby, but as of Thursday (Nov. 5), they can rejoice at the […]
articles.content: Good Truckin’ Diner’s departure from its original location in REO Town must have stung for those who live nearby, but as of Thursday (Nov. 5), they can rejoice at the business’ return to their side of town in the form of Good Truckin’ REO Bites — and we can all rejoice in exploring the new favorites this fresh venture brings. Jalapeno Business at REO Bites in Old Town. Photo by Lizy Ferguson for City Pulse REO Bites offers breakfast sandwiches, subs, tacos and hot dogs, as well as an ice cream menu with soft serve, shakes and floats. As much as a spaghetti taco or a pimento cheese and bacon jam hot dog intrigued me, I was (and always am) in the mood for a big sandwich. I was torn between the Bodega, with chopped beef and cheese sauce, and the Jalapeno Business, with turkey, provolone and poblano aioli. However, I had a suspicion that the turkey might be actual roast turkey instead of deli slices, so I took a leap of faith. The toasted hoagie did, in fact, come with a generous portion of roast turkey, topped with the aforementioned provolone and aioli as well as candied jalapeno, tomato and lettuce. The bread was a little on the limp side, but everything it held was delicious. The turkey was thick-cut, flavorful and juicy, and the sweet-and-spicy jalapeños were the perfect contrast to the rich and smoky poblano sauce, with the abundance of melty provolone tying everything together. I hope REO Bites eventually adds fries to its menu, but for now it does have chips, in addition to house-made mac and cheese and coleslaw. The sandwich was definitely more than satisfying on its own, though, and if you have to go back to work after ordering one, I’d recommend saving half for later, lest you succumb to sleepiness. You aren’t in Old Town on a Sunday, after all. You’re in REO Town, and it’s 11:30 a.m. on a Tuesday. A Faygo float won’t hurt, though. Jalapeno Business $12 Good Truckin’ REO Bites 1107 S. Washington Ave., Lansing 11 a.m.-7 p.m. Tuesday-Friday 9 a.m.-4 p.m. Saturday (517) 489-2070 Good Truckin’ continues to impress in new Old Town digs
