articles.title: Call him Mr. Soccer: De La Salle’s Andrew Corder earns prestigious award
articles.content: It doesn’t seem that long ago when Andrew Corder scored his first career varsity goal. “It came against Harbor Springs at the Boyne Invitational my freshman year,” recalled Corder, who is now a senior at Warren De La Salle. “It doesn’t seem that long ago.” Well, Corder went on to score 103 career goals and a boatload of game-winning goals as well, including Saturday’s third goal in the Division 2 state finals – a 3-2 victory over top-ranked St. Joseph at Grand Ledge High School – which helped jettison the talented Pilots to their eighth overall state title. Corder’s brilliant four-year varsity career – he never did leave De La Salle for any MLS Next Academy programs – included four district titles, four regional championships, four appearances in the Division 2 Final Four, and three straight Division 2 state championships in 2024, 2025 and 2026. “It’s been a great four years. It kind of stinks that I won’t be able to play for De La Salle anymore. My teammates have been perfect and my coaches have been perfect. But I guess it’s been a great time, and I am honored to win this award,” said Corder Tuesday evening just shortly after the Michigan High School Soccer Coaches Association announced its Mr. Soccer award winner and 11-member All-State Dream Team selections. The Dream Team features 10 field players and one goalkeeper each year from each of the MHSAA’s four divisions. “My coach called me Sunday night and I suspected he was going to tell me that I won it and he did. But I was told that I could not tell anyone and could not (share on social media) until it was (officially announced) that I won the award,” noted Corder. “I felt like this was going to happen.” Corder, who scored 32 goals as a senior this season and had over 30 game-winning goals during his four-year career, will be issued the Mr. Soccer trophy at the Michigan High School Soccer Coaches Association banquet later this month. He is just the second Mr. Soccer award winner to hail from De La Salle – with Brian Maisonneuve being the other in 1990 after Maisonneuve led the Pilots to a 24-1-0 record and the Class A state championship, the first of eight state titles in De La Salle’s illustrious history. “He’s special,” admitted veteran De La Salle coach Thaier Mukhtar. “In all of my years of coaching soccer, I’ve only really pushed for three players to be a candidate for Mr. Soccer – Brian Maisonneuve, Spencer Thompson and now Andrew Corder. “Brian won Mr. Soccer a long time ago and played for (the U.S. Men’s National Team) in the World Cup. Spencer Thompson ended up third (in the Mr. Soccer voting) and went on to be a four-year starter for Michigan State, and now Andrew Corder has had a great career at De La Salle and won it. Andrew broke Brian Maisonneuve’s (career) scoring record and now he’s the best player in the state.” Corder is the first player in Michigan over the past 40 years to come from a Class A, Class B, Division 1 or Division 2 program to earn All-State First Team honors as well. He has accepted an invitation to compete in the National High School Soccer Coaches Association All-Star game and will be a shoe-in to earn NSHSCA All-America honors this season along with being a candidate for Gatorade Michigan Player of the Year, which will be announced next spring. On this year’s All-State Dream Team, Corder is joined by Clinton Township Chippewa Valley senior forward Joey Garner, Grand Rapids Christian senior midfielder Liam Jansen, St. Joseph senior midfielder Evan Hudak, Detroit U-D Jesuit senior midfielder Vasco Marra, Allendale senior midfielder Kolby Mallott, Plymouth Salem senior forward Tyler Varesh, Troy sophomore forward Connor Hotts, Elk Rapids senior midfielder Drew Plum, Royal Oak senior midfielder Baylor Brownrigg and Ann Arbor Skyline senior goalkeeper Jack Collins. The All-State First Team, All-State Second Team, All-State Third Team and All-State Honorable Mention lists in each of the state’s four divisions will be released this week as well on the coaches’ association’s website at www.https://mihssca.com. Corder has received interest from NCAA Division I schools University of Detroit Mercy, Western Michigan University, University of Dayton, Ohio State University, and Bowling Green State University amongst others as well as dozens of NCAA Division II and Division III programs from around the Midwest and country. He is still waiting to see what offers are on the table following the NCAA Division I schools sorting through the transfer portal and filling the fifth-year seniors on their respective rosters before they dip into the pool of high school seniors. Chippewa Valley’s Joey Garner was second in the Mr. Soccer voting and was named the top field player in Division 1 this season. That gives Macomb County the top two players in the Mr. Soccer voting and spots on the Dream Team for the first time as the aforementioned Andrew Corder topped the list. Garner, who committed to NCAA Division I Oakland University in October of last year, picked up some serious interest from other Power 4 conference schools over the last year. He led Chippewa Valley to its first district title since 2019 and scored 29 goals this season. Garner was All-State Third Team as a junior. He is the first Chippewa Valley player to earn Dream Team status since Nick DeGraw was named Mr. Soccer back in 1998.

As Greenland’s climate changes, a new project preserves memories of a fading past
articles.content: ILULISSAT, Greenland (AP) — When Cuno Jensen was a child, he would watch towering icebergs drift past his hometown, flowing out into Disko Bay. “When we were kids, and we walked up there with our family or hunting for some of the birds, we saw huge icebergs,” he said as he drove through Ilulissat on Greenland’s western coast, about 300 kilometers (185 miles) north of the Arctic Circle. “And nowadays, when we look at the scenery … we can see some of the icebergs (but) not that tall or big as it used to be.” Greenland is hard hit by climate change, the focus of an annual United Nations conference opening in Turkey this week. Thanks in large part to climate change, driven by the burning of oil, gas and coal, the Arctic is warming four times faster than the rest of the planet. Recollections like Jensen’s feature in a new project called “Mapping Memories,” led by Sweden-based research institute Nordregio, which aims to build and preserve a lasting record of the past before it’s too late. Icebergs drifting in the Ilulissat Icefjord near Ilulissat, Greenland, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/James Brooks) Icebergs drifting in the Ilulissat Icefjord near Ilulissat, Greenland, Wednesday, Nov. 4, 2026. (AP Photo/James Brooks) An exhibit linked to the project opened in September at Ilulissat’s Icefjord Center, billed as Greenland’s first visitor center, that is devoted to exploring the link between people and nature. “If we do not document the people’s own stories, they will disappear when the people pass away,” said Karl Sandgreen, the center’s director. “We wanted to have the ordinary people’s experiences,” he said. “All the facts we get are told by the scientists, archaeologists, glaciologists, biologists. … We also want to have another perspective to document climate change.” As Greenland’s ice melts, landscape shifts and climate changes. Jensen, a burly, 42-year-old father of three, said he fears his young children will not experience the same things he did. “When we were kids playing around these hills, there was much more snow and the water was frozen and it was ice,” said Jensen, a corrections officer. “We could get out on the ice and fish. That’s nothing we can do today.” Cuno Jensen, a 42-year-old prison worker poses for a photo in Ilulissat, Greenland, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/James Brooks) Cuno Jensen, a 42-year-old prison worker poses for a photo in Ilulissat, Greenland, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/James Brooks) Across the icy territory, climate change is not only transforming the landscape but eroding memories and traditions tied to it. Thinning sea ice means some hunters can no longer ride their dog sleds. Waters are becoming less predictable for the island’s traditional fishermen. So far, the “Mapping Memories” project features nearly 60 personal stories — including Jensen’s — tied to specific locations in Greenland. Some describe homes threatened by thawing permafrost and changing weather conditions. Others document disappearing traditions and hunting routes. View inside the exhibition “Mapping Memories” at the Ilulissat Icefjord Center in Ilulissat, Greenland, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/James Brooks) View inside the exhibition “Mapping Memories” at the Ilulissat Icefjord Center in Ilulissat, Greenland, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/James Brooks) Fisherwoman Karen Alaufesen recalls a spot at sea where she fishes for halibut with her husband and young son. Their numbers have been declining, she said. Pensioner Kristian Petersen remembers his former hometown of Qullissat, a coal-mining settlement abandoned in 1972 after its mine closed. Six years ago, the abandoned town was struck by a devastating tsunami triggered by a landslide. In Ilulissat, rising temperatures are thawing permafrost, causing buildings to sink and roads and pipes to crack. “Everybody can see a lot of buildings are sinking,” said Sandgreen, pointing to the town’s 19th-century history museum, its wooden staircase slanted as the grounds beneath it shift. “It is very, very easy to spot.” Archaeological objects, including hunting tools dating back 4,000 years, are also emerging from the ice, he added. General view on the village Ilulissat, Greenland, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/James Brooks) General view on the village Ilulissat, Greenland, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026. (AP Photo/James Brooks) The nearby Sermeq Kujalleq glacier is one of the fastest-moving and most active on the planet, sending more icebergs into the sea than any other glacier outside Antarctica, according to United Nations cultural organization UNESCO. As the climate has warmed, the glacier has retreated and calved off chunks of ice faster than ever before, significantly contributing to sea level rise from Europe to the Pacific Islands, according to NASA. A September report by the Geological Survey of Denmark and Greenland said the Greenland ice sheet, a 1.7-million-square-kilometer (660,000-square-mile) ice sheet covering about 80% of the Arctic island, has now lost more ice than it has gained for 30 years in a row. Signe Hillerup Larsen, a senior researcher at the survey, said she sees no scenario in which the ice sheet could regain its lost mass, let alone begin growing again. “Even if it (the melting) would be slowing down, that would not be enough,” she said. Sandgreen said organizers plan to expand the project with more interviews, including with communities in nearby Canada, and add them to an interactive map. They also want to inspire kids to do more to fight climate change. “We want to develop it so all the people who have experienced this melting permafrost and climate change have a chance to tell their stories,” he said.
